title: LEEDUCA Platform Technical Manual
text:
Preface
The LEEDUCA/PRELEO platform assesses children aged 3 to 11 in schools in Málaga (Spain) online, three times per school year (3-year-olds since 2023/24). It covers letter knowledge, phonological awareness, rapid automatized naming, word and text reading, reading comprehension, oral language, mathematics and executive functions. Since 2014 it has gathered data from several birth cohorts, named by their year of birth (2010, 2011, 2012…).
The manual describes every task on the platform with the same structure: what it measures and how it is administered, the sample it has been studied in, its reliability and validity, how its scores are interpreted (norms), and which variables affect them. It is written for three kinds of readers:

title: LEEDUCA Platform Technical Manual
text:
Origins
The platform and this manual grew out of the DIS-ESP battery, created by María Soledad Carrillo (University of Murcia, a member of the group) and Jesús Alegría (Université Libre de Bruxelles). DIS-ESP proposed a two-stage assessment of dyslexia: group screening of reading efficiency with TECLE and, for the children it flagged, an assessment of the two reading mechanisms, phonological and orthographic (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011). The LEEDUCA group promoted it in Málaga on paper (2007–2012) and then moved it to an online platform, which added the early literacy precursors from age 4 and assessment three times per school year.

title: LEEDUCA Platform Technical Manual
text:
How to read this book
Each task sheet has three layers:

The text, with the results and what they mean.
The full tables, at the end of each sheet. They are read from the files in datos/agregados/, which contain only aggregated results (means, percentiles, correlations…), never data from an individual child.
The code, in the GitHub repository (button in the sidebar). Tables are computed with R scripts from the complete data, which for privacy reasons never leave the project’s computer. The book is built from those tables, so anyone can reproduce its figures.

title: LEEDUCA Platform Technical Manual
text:
Privacy
This book contains only aggregated data. Pupils’ names and identification numbers, teachers’ names and individual data stay in the project folder at the University of Málaga. Teachers always appear under pseudonyms. Norms of commercial tests used for comparison (PROLEC-R, EDICOLE) are not reproduced, only cited.

title: Technical summary (English)
text:
The LEEDUCA platform
LEEDUCA is an online assessment platform for reading and its precursors in children aged 3 to 11, developed by the LEEDUCA research group at the University of Málaga (Spain). It grew out of the paper-based DIS-ESP battery (M. S. Carrillo and J. Alegría), which proposed a two-stage assessment of dyslexia in a transparent orthography (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011). The platform is used in schools three times per school year (autumn, winter and spring). Most tasks are administered individually by a trained examiner at a computer; the platform presents the stimuli, records responses and item-level response times, and produces reports.
Domains covered: letter knowledge, phonological awareness, rapid automatized naming (RAN), verbal short-term memory, word and pseudoword reading, text reading fluency, reading comprehension, oral language (vocabulary, morphosyntax, comprehension), numerical cognition and executive functions.

title: Technical summary (English)
text:
Normative sample
The normative study uses six birth cohorts (2010–2015) assessed in schools of the province of Málaga: 10,278 children (31 to 72 schools per cohort). Of these, 4,952 were followed term by term until 2019/20; the remainder were assessed only in the broad assessments of 2020/21 (paper) and 2021/22 (tablets). Part of the schools applied Preleo, a classroom program for oral language and early literacy. Norms use children from schools without Preleo as the reference group (1,628 children in term-by-term follow-up); when a time point has fewer than 100 reference children, all children are used and this is flagged. A flow diagram is given in Normative study.

title: Technical summary (English)
text:
Psychometric approach

Scores by task family. Tasks are grouped into seven families according to how they measure (accuracy, RAN, oral reading fluency, timed efficiency, timed decision, span, comprehension). The family determines the main score and the reliability method.
Reliability. Internal consistency (α, ω) only for untimed accuracy tasks; test–retest and parallel forms for speeded tasks. Every percentile is reported with a 90 % confidence band.
Validity. Content (items and instructions read from the platform), internal structure (exploratory factor and network analyses by age), external criterion (Woodcock-Muñoz fluency), and predictive and diagnostic validity against persistent reading difficulty, with cross-validation leaving one cohort out. Precursors at age 5 (phonological awareness, letter knowledge and RAN) predict persistent difficulty with an AUC of .82 (.73 at age 4); letters and phonological awareness carry most of the weight.
Norms by school term. Because children change fast between 4 and 7, norms are given by school year and term; continuous norms are under development.
Quality classes. Each task is classed A (sufficient reliability, validity and norms for individual use), B (use with caution) or C (research or description only). There are 32 class A tasks; 98 tasks have an automatically generated technical sheet.

title: Technical summary (English)
text:
Risk classification
Reading difficulty is defined from the child’s whole trajectory between 6 and 11 years, not from a single assessment, in five certainty levels: severe persistent reading difficulty (DL-A: ≤ P10 in at least two school years and ≤ P25 in all years from age 7), persistent reading difficulty (DL-B), transient difficulty (TR), intermediate (INT) and stable typical (TE). The same logic is proposed for oral language and mathematics. Term reports use five bands with a watch zone between P20 and P30, where no label is given until the next assessment; in simulations with reliability .85, this halves label changes due to measurement error alone (from 14 % to 6 %).

title: Technical summary (English)
text:
Intended uses
Supported: universal screening (as a probability of risk), progress monitoring, planning classroom support, and research with pseudonymized data. Not supported: clinical diagnosis on its own, high-stakes decisions about individual children, and comparison of schools or teachers. See Presentation and responsible use.

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
What the platform is
In one sentence. The LEEDUCA platform is for early identification, monitoring progress and deciding on support in the classroom. It is not, on its own, for diagnosis, and its scores are always interpreted with their margin of error, by professionals with appropriate training and with respect for the rights of children and their families.
LEEDUCA is an online assessment battery of reading and its precursors for children aged 3 to 11. It is administered at school, three times per school year, with brief tasks of letter knowledge, phonological awareness, rapid naming, word, pseudoword and text reading, comprehension, oral language, numerical cognition and executive functions. The platform presents the stimuli, records responses and times item by item, and generates reports. Its history and how it works are described in The LEEDUCA platform.
This manual is its technical documentation: it describes each task, the sample in which it has been studied, its reliability and validity, its norms and the limits of each score. It follows the logic of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, and National Council on Measurement in Education 2014): a test is not validated in the abstract, but each proposed use of its scores, with the evidence that supports it (Kane 2013).

Who can use it

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Administering well
The validity of a score starts with its administration. The guidelines on computer-based and internet testing (International Test Commission 2006) and the experience with the platform lead to these conditions:

Place. A quiet space in the school, without other children watching, with a checked computer and headphones for tasks with recorded stimuli.
Mode. Most tasks are individual with an examiner: the examiner follows the platform’s instruction, does not help or give hints, and marks the response exactly as the child gives it. Group or self-administered tasks are indicated in their task sheet.
Timing. Within the window for each term, so that the norms for that time point are appropriate.
Incidents. If a child gets tired or distracted, or there is a technical failure, it is noted and the session is flagged for review. Detectors of anomalous sessions help to find them (see 5.1 Scores).
Accommodations. A child with a sensory or motor impairment, or who is learning Spanish, may need accommodations. If the administration is changed, the score is no longer comparable with the norms, and the report says so.

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Interpreting well

A score is an estimate with error. Each percentile is read with its confidence band. The same child can score differently in two assessments without having changed (see The dancing percentile (in Spanish)).
Near the cut-off, monitor. Between P20 and P30 no label is given: the child’s progress is checked at the next assessment (see The watch zone (in Spanish)).
Risk is a probability, not a diagnosis. A sentence such as “of every 100 children with this profile, about 22 will have difficulties” is better understood and less misleading than “at risk”.
A single task is not enough. The decision rests on the profile, the teacher’s judgment and the response to instruction.
Context matters. Before interpreting a low result, what is not reading is ruled out: little schooling, a different home language, hearing or vision problems, a bad session.
Progress counts as much as level. A child below the average who grows more than expected is responding to instruction.

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Communicating with families
Families have the right to understandable and useful information. The proposed family report gives three things: where the child stands (with its interval), how the child is progressing and what is going to be done, with a date to look again. It avoids diagnostic labels, explains that a result on a given day can vary and suggests simple activities for home. A worrying result is communicated in person, by the class teacher or the school psychologist, and not only in writing.

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Ethics and data protection
The platform processes data from minors, who have reinforced protection. Processing is governed by the General Data Protection Regulation (Parlamento Europeo y Consejo de la Unión Europea 2016) and the Spanish Organic Law 3/2018 (Jefatura del Estado 2018). The principles the manual follows:

Purpose. Data are collected to assess and support reading development at school. Their use in research requires families’ consent for that purpose and the corresponding ethics approval.
Minimization and pseudonymization. The manual and its analyses use a pseudonymized identifier. Names, pupil identification numbers and teachers’ names do not leave the project folder at the University of Málaga. Teachers always appear under pseudonyms.
Only aggregated data in public. This book publishes means, percentiles and correlations, never data from a single child. No table allows a pupil, a class or a teacher to be identified.
Tiered access. Open (this book), under a data use agreement (pseudonymized long table) and restricted (original exports). See Research with the platform data (in Spanish).
To be confirmed: families’ informed consent procedure in each cohort; the ethics committee that approved the project and its reference; data controller and data retention period.

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Test security
Tasks lose value if their items circulate. That is why the manual does not reproduce the full reading lists or the task items: screenshots show at most the example or the first two items, and item properties are summarized by list. Norms of commercial tests used as criteria (for example, Woodcock-Muñoz, PROLEC-R or EDICOLE) are not reproduced; they are only cited (Muñiz, Hernández, and Ponsoda 2015).

title: Presentation and responsible use
text:
Fairness
A fair test measures the same thing and makes the same errors in all groups. The manual checks, task by task, whether a score works the same by sex, school socioeconomic status, format (platform, paper or tablet) and period (before and after the pandemic), and whether the same cut-off is equally accurate in all groups (see 5.6 Fairness). Until this is checked, results for children who are learning Spanish and for the Catalan and Valencian versions are interpreted with caution. The same applies to dialectal variation in the phonological and spelling tasks: with seseo or ceceo (merging /s/ and /θ/), common in Málaga, some responses may not mean the same as in a child who distinguishes /s/ and /θ/ (see Spelling words).

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
text:
Learning to read in a transparent orthography
In one sentence. In Spanish, almost all children learn to decode in their first school year; what separates good readers from those with difficulties is, above all, how quickly they come to read automatically, and this can be anticipated from preschool with a few precursors.
In Spanish, each letter or group of letters is almost always pronounced the same way. This transparency changes the course of learning compared with English:
What it implies for the platform. Speed must be measured as well as accuracy, and several times per school year, because change between ages 5 and 8 is very fast. Words reflect the orthographic lexicon already built and pseudowords, pure decoding. The difficulty of a word does not depend only on its length, but also on when it is learned orally and how many words resemble it (Alonso, Fernández, and Díez 2015) (see What makes a word list difficult (in Spanish)).
crumbs: 2  Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
text:
Decoding is mastered early. In a study of 13 European orthographies, children learning transparent languages such as Spanish read more than 90% of simple words and pseudowords correctly at the end of their first school year; children learning English, less than 40% (Seymour, Aro, and Erskine 2003). Accuracy quickly stops distinguishing children from one another.
What remains is fluency. After mastering the code, the child has to read faster and with less effort. In a transparent orthography, individual differences lie mainly in speed and are very stable: those who read slowly in Grade 1 usually still read slowly years later (Landerl and Wimmer 2008).
The reader teaches themselves. Each time a child decodes a word, something of its written form is stored. After a few exposures, the word is recognized at a glance (Share 1995). That is why decoding is the gateway to the orthographic lexicon, not a stage that is left behind (Ehri 2005).
The size of the unit changes. At first, reading is letter by letter; with practice, the child uses larger units (syllables, morphemes, whole words) (Ziegler and Goswami 2005). That is why the word length effect is large at first and decreases over the years, and is larger in children with difficulties (Zoccolotti et al. 2005; Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007).
Automatization frees resources. When decoding is automatic, attention is free for comprehension (LaBerge and Samuels 1974). Those who read slowly read less, and those who read less fall further behind: differences tend to grow over the years (Stanovich 1986).
crumbs: 2  Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
text:
From decoding to comprehension
The simple view of reading proposes that reading comprehension is the product of two skills: decoding and oral language comprehension (Gough and Tunmer 1986; Hoover and Gough 1990). If either fails, comprehension fails. At first decoding weighs more; over the years, once decoding is automatic, oral language weighs more and more: vocabulary, grammar and world knowledge (Storch and Whitehurst 2002; Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018).
What it implies for the platform. Reading comprehension cannot be interpreted without knowing how the child decodes. A child who understands poorly because they read slowly needs different help from one who reads well but does not understand. That is why the platform measures decoding, speed, comprehension and oral language separately, and the manual proposes treating comprehension as a separate dimension (see How we estimate risk).
crumbs: 2  Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
section: Spelling words: the same code in the opposite direction
text:
Spelling words: the same code in the opposite direction
Reading and spelling words rely on the same knowledge: the correspondences between letters and sounds and the written forms stored in the orthographic lexicon. But they are not equally hard. To read, it is enough to recognize the word; to spell it, all its letters must be retrieved, in order. A representation that is enough to read a word may not be enough to spell it correctly (Perfetti 1997).

Spanish is more transparent for reading than for spelling. Almost every letter is read in only one way, but several sounds can be written in more than one: /b/ with b or v, /x/ with j or with g before e and i, /ʝ/ with ll or y, and h is silent. Some spellings depend on a context rule (c/qu, g/gu, r/rr); others only on knowing the word. In a sample of 1,045 children in Grades 2 to 6, the spelling of these words was not mastered until Grade 4 or 5, and the most frequent errors involved b/v, h and c/s/z/x (Jiménez et al. 2008).
Word spelling is learned through reading. Each correctly decoded word leaves a trace of its written form (Share 1995). In Spanish, this orthographic lexicon forms earlier than in French: the effect of word frequency on spelling, which indicates that the word’s form is stored, appears earlier in Spanish children than in French children (Carrillo, Alegría, and Marín 2013). Spelling mechanisms are the same in all alphabetic orthographies; in Spanish they are acquired faster (Alegría and Carrillo 2014). From Grade 2, children also use regularities that do not belong to any particular word: they choose b or v according to how frequent each combination with the following vowel is (at the start of a word, vi is more frequent than bi, and bu more than vu) (Carrillo and Alegría 2014).
The precursors are the same. Phonemic awareness, letter knowledge and rapid naming predict both word reading and word spelling, in Spanish and in other alphabetic orthographies (Caravolas et al. 2012).
Reading and spelling can fail separately. In a representative sample of 2,029 German-speaking children, another transparent orthography, 7% had an isolated reading deficit and 6% an isolated spelling deficit (Moll and Landerl 2009). These profiles partly persist throughout primary school (Moll et al. 2020). A screening that only looks at reading misses children whose difficulty lies mainly in spelling. That is why the new IDA definition includes spelling (International Dyslexia Association 2025).
Teaching spelling also helps reading. In a meta-analysis of 53 studies, explicit spelling instruction improved word spelling and, in addition, phonological awareness and reading (Graham and Santangelo 2014).

A note on the speech of Málaga. With seseo or ceceo, s, c (before e and i) and z represent the same sound for many children. For them, Spanish has one more inconsistency in spelling. The Tenerife study, also an area of seseo, found many c/s/z errors in dictation (Jiménez et al. 2008), but did not compare varieties. It is a hypothesis the manual would need to test before norming a dictation task: c/s/z errors by a child with seseo do not mean the same as those by a child who distinguishes the two sounds.

crumbs: 2  Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
text:
Morphology: meaning within the word
Morphemes are the smallest units with meaning: the root pan (bread) in panadero (baker) and empanada, the suffix -ero that forms occupations, the plural -s or the feminine -a. Spanish has a rich morphology in the two senses that matter here:

Inflectional: gender and number in nouns, adjectives and determiners, which must also agree (las casas blancas, the white houses), and a verb conjugation with many forms (canto, cantaba, cantaré, cante).
Derivational: prefixes and suffixes that form new words from a base (leer → lector, lectura, releer, ilegible; read → reader, reading, reread, illegible).

Morphological awareness is the ability to notice that structure and use it: recognizing that panadero contains pan, forming the plural of an invented word, or working out what despeinable means without ever having heard it.

Why the IDA places it next to phonology
The new IDA definition states that underlying difficulties in phonological and morphological processing are common but not universal, and that early oral language weakness often foreshadows problems with reading and spelling (International Dyslexia Association 2025; Catts, Haynes, and Joshi 2026). The committee included morphology to underline its role in reading and spelling across languages and writing systems. In the prior consultation, a quarter of the participants did not want a definition limited to the “phonological component”, because it left out other language difficulties such as morphological awareness. The British definition, on the other hand, only raises phonological processing to that category (Carroll et al. 2025) (see What we measure in light of the new definition).
The empirical basis is broad:

Morphology is related to everything that is read and written. A meta-analysis of 232 articles and almost 50,000 participants in 17 languages found moderate correlations of morphological awareness with phonological awareness (r = .41), vocabulary (.50), word reading (.49), spelling (.48), text fluency (.53) and comprehension (.54) (Lee, Wolters, and Kim 2022). Longitudinal studies confirm that the relation holds over time (Manolitsis et al. 2019).
It links sound, written form and meaning. A morpheme is represented in both speech and writing, and it carries a meaning. That is why morphological knowledge can help in several ways: to recognize words more efficiently and to comprehend, because it allows the meaning and grammatical function of unknown words to be inferred (Bowers, Kirby, and Deacon 2010). Morphology has thus been proposed to act as a “glue” that binds the three aspects of each word (Kirby and Bowers 2017).
It still matters in the higher grades. In 126 Canadian children followed from Grade 3 to Grade 5, morphological awareness, rapid naming and phonological awareness each contributed to word reading, speed and comprehension, controlling for verbal and nonverbal ability. They also explained how much each child improved between those grades beyond what their Grade 3 level predicted. Morphology weighed most in comprehension (Kirby et al. 2025). Its improvement between Grades 3 and 5 also translated into better reading, so it is not a trait fixed at the start of primary school.
Children with dyslexia have lower morphological awareness than peers of the same age, with a large effect (g = 1.11 in 40 studies), of the same size as for phonological awareness or rapid naming. But they do not have lower morphological awareness than younger children of the same reading level (g = −0.08) (Georgiou et al. 2022). The authors conclude that morphological awareness is not a central causal feature of dyslexia; one possible explanation is that it develops through reading, and those who read less develop it less. This fits with what the manual says about dyslexia in Spanish as a delay rather than a deviance (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007) and with the IDA’s “common but not universal”.



Morphology in a transparent orthography
In English, morphology helps with pronunciation: heal and health share a root even though the vowel sounds different. In Spanish this is hardly needed, because letter-to-sound conversion rules are enough to read almost any word aloud. That is why the role of morphology shifts:

It weighs less in reading accuracy. The relation between morphological awareness and word reading is weaker in transparent orthographies (r = .38) than in opaque ones (.52) (Lee, Wolters, and Kim 2022).
It weighs in speed. In Argentine children in Grades 2 to 6, words with morphological structure were read faster, but not with fewer errors, in all grades (D’Alessio, Jaichenco, and Wilson 2018). This is to be expected if the morpheme is one of the large units the reader increasingly uses while automatizing (Ziegler and Goswami 2005). And, in a transparent orthography, the difficulty lies mainly in speed (see Above all, slowness).
It weighs in comprehension. In Grade 4, morphological awareness predicted reading comprehension directly and not through decoding, unlike in English (D’Alessio, Jaichenco, and Wilson 2019). Morphology gives access to the meaning and grammatical function of new words.
It weighs in spelling. Many of the inconsistent spellings of Spanish are kept within a word family (vaca, vaquero, vaquería; hacer, deshacer, rehacer), and some depend on a morpheme (the imperfect past -aba is always spelled with b). Knowing that two words share a root is a clue to spelling them correctly.
It also weighs at the start. In pointed Hebrew, a very transparent orthography, morphological awareness measured in preschool predicted reading accuracy and fluency in the middle of Grade 1, even controlling for phonemic awareness (Cohen-Mimran et al. 2022).

Readers with dyslexia in Spanish. Spanish children with dyslexia aged 7 to 10 read words and pseudowords with morphological structure better than simple ones: they use the morpheme as a unit larger than the letter to get around their decoding difficulty (Suárez-Coalla and Cuetos 2013). But they take less advantage of it than their peers: in a lexical decision task, only typical readers of the same age benefited from a frequent root (Lázaro, Camacho, and Burani 2013). In adolescents with dyslexia, recognizing the root is a compensatory strategy when reading words and texts (Elbro and Arnbak 1996). In university students with dyslexia, morphological awareness can be preserved even though phonological awareness remains low, and the larger that gap, the better they read (Cavalli et al. 2017). Both results point to morphology as a compensation route. It is the kind of strength the IDA asks to be identified and used.


Before reading: inflectional morphology, vocabulary and phonological awareness
In preschool, the morphology that can be measured is mainly inflectional and oral: forming the plural or the feminine, or recognizing the correct form. Its relation with reading runs through oral language and through phonological awareness itself.

The lexical restructuring hypothesis. As vocabulary grows, the child needs increasingly detailed representations of words to tell them apart. That pressure pushes toward smaller units, such as syllables and phonemes, and prepares phonological awareness (Metsala and Walley 1998).
Morphology as a link. The doctoral thesis of María Rodríguez-Moreno, supervised in the LEEDUCA group, extends that hypothesis with tasks from the platform itself (Rodríguez-Moreno 2026). It proposes that vocabulary opens two routes to phonological awareness. One is direct: more words require finer representations. The other is indirect: the more words a child knows, the more examples they have to discover that certain sound changes go together with changes in meaning (gato–gatos, cat–cats; alto–alta, tall masc.–fem.; salta–saltó, jumps–jumped). Noticing those changing parts would make the internal structure of the word more accessible and prepare the conscious analysis of its sounds.

Cross-sectional study (452 children from 30 schools in Málaga, mean age 4;11). Verbal inflectional morphology explained unique variance in syllable and rhyme awareness, beyond vocabulary, age, socioeconomic status, verbal memory and minimal-pair discrimination. The indirect effect of vocabulary through morphology was positive in all models.
Longitudinal study (291 children, five assessments over 15 months, from 3;2 to 4;3 years). Early vocabulary predicted later gender, number and verb tense. Gender (at 4;1) and number (at 4;2) predicted final phonological awareness, controlling for the initial level. The indirect effect of vocabulary through gender was small but significant: β = .077 for syllables and .050 for rhymes.
The relations run in both directions. In the cross-sectional study, the reverse order, with syllable awareness in the middle, also fit the data. In the longitudinal study, an exploratory route appeared from early syllable awareness to later vocabulary, through morphology. The thesis itself warns that its studies are observational: it remains to be shown, with an intervention, that working on inflection improves phonological awareness.

An early indicator of language risk. In children at family risk of dyslexia, inflection at age 2 already predicted language at age 5; in controls it did not until 3;6 (Lyytinen and Lyytinen 2004). In Spanish, preschoolers with developmental language disorder (DLD) use grammatical morphology worse than peers of the same age and younger children of the same language level, especially adjective agreement and object clitics (Bedore and Leonard 2001). In Spanish–English bilingual children aged 4 to 6, accuracy on verbs and the subjunctive distinguished children with DLD well (Castilla-Earls et al. 2021). For the platform, low inflectional morphology at ages 3–5 is above all a sign about oral language (see Screening for two risks).



Teaching morphology
Explicit morphology instruction improves literacy. In 30 studies in English, the mean effect was d = 0.32; it was larger for decoding (0.59) and phonological awareness (0.48), and not significant for comprehension or fluency (Goodwin and Ahn 2013). It especially benefits struggling readers and works better combined with the rest of reading instruction (Bowers, Kirby, and Deacon 2010). Almost all studies are in English, so the effect size in Spanish remains to be tested. Preleo already includes compound words and word families in its vocabulary block (see Preleo), and its effectiveness when delivered by teachers themselves in preschool is documented (Sánchez-Gómez et al. 2025). María’s thesis proposes a further step in preschool: choosing words and situations in which the sound change matters for understanding the message (a picture with one cat or several; el niño alto and la niña alta, the tall boy and the tall girl; hoy salta and ayer saltó, today he jumps and yesterday he jumped). Then gradually moving from use to noticing which part of the word stays and which changes (Rodríguez-Moreno 2026). It is an applied hypothesis that the thesis proposes to test with a trial comparing two versions of the program.
What it implies for the platform. Today the platform only measures oral inflectional morphology in preschool and at the start of Grade 1. It does not measure derivational or written morphology, which are the ones most related to fluency, comprehension and spelling from Grade 2:

These tasks originated in the block of language hypotheses and comorbidity with DLD, and that is where they fit best: as part of the oral language component of screening, not as an indicator of a morphological cause of dyslexia. The pseudoword tasks are the closest to morphological awareness, because the child cannot rely on a memorized form.
What is missing is a derivational morphology task, oral in preschool and written in primary school, to follow children in the grades in which morphology weighs most in comprehension (Kirby et al. 2025): forming derived words (pan → panadero), breaking them down, or deciding between pseudowords with and without a real suffix. The diagnostic summary chart used by the group already records derivational and inflectional morphology, and it considers a morphological cause in the child’s profile, but today there is no platform task to fill in the derivational box. With it, the manual could identify children with a morphological difficulty and also those for whom it is a strength.

The precursors: what can be measured before reading
Before children read, several skills anticipate how they will learn. The same predictors work in transparent and opaque orthographies, although their weight changes with age and language (Caravolas et al. 2013; Landerl et al. 2013).



Precursor
What it is
Why it predicts
Where it is in the manual




Letter knowledge
Letter names and sounds
It is the basis of letter–sound correspondences and reflects exposure to print (Foulin 2005)
Letter knowledge


Phonological awareness
Noticing and manipulating the sounds of words: syllables, rhymes and phonemes
It allows sounds to be segmented and blended, which is what decoding requires; it mainly predicts early accuracy (Landerl et al. 2019)
Phonological awareness


Rapid automatized naming (RAN)
Naming a series of colors, objects, digits or letters as fast as possible
It reflects how fast visual and phonological information are connected; it mainly predicts fluency (Norton and Wolf 2012; Landerl et al. 2019)
Rapid naming


Verbal short-term memory
Repeating series of words or syllables
It holds sounds while decoding
Verbal memory task sheets


Oral language
Vocabulary, morphology, syntax and oral comprehension
It is the other half of reading comprehension (Storch and Whitehurst 2002)
Oral language task sheets



In general, phonological awareness weighs more at the start of learning and rapid naming gains weight once reading depends on speed (Landerl et al. 2019). In the platform data, letters and phonological awareness at age 5 anticipate persistent difficulty with an area under the curve of .82 (see How we estimate risk).

title: Theoretical framework: learning to read in Spanish and why we measure what we measure
text:
Reading difficulty in Spanish

Above all, slowness
In transparent orthographies, dyslexia shows mainly as slow and laborious reading, with relatively few errors. Spanish children with dyslexia read with accuracy close to that of their peers, but much more slowly, and the word length effect is larger in them (Serrano and Defior 2008; Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A child can read “well” if only errors are counted and still have a serious difficulty. That is why the platform measures the time for each item and not only correct responses.


Above all, a delay
When children with dyslexia are compared with younger children who read at the same level, their profiles are very similar: in Spanish, dyslexia behaves more like a delay than a different development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). The classic “subtypes” (phonological and surface) depend heavily on the method and the comparison group. With age-matched controls many appear; with reading-level controls, far fewer (Carrillo Gallego, Alegría, and Calvo Rodríguez 2008; Sprenger-Charolles 2011).


Several factors, not a single cause
Dyslexia is not explained by a single deficit. It results from several risk factors (phonological, processing speed, oral language, familial and environmental) that add up and can be offset by protective factors (Pennington 2006; Catts et al. 2017). The cumulative risk and resilience model draws a practical consequence from this: risk is better estimated by adding indicators than by looking for a single one, and it is expressed as a probability (Catts and Petscher 2022). The phonological deficit is common but does not explain all cases: some children have mainly a speed problem, which shows in rapid naming (Wimmer, Mayringer, and Landerl 2000).


A continuum, not a category
Reading ability is continuously distributed. Where the cut-off is placed is a decision, and prevalence depends on that decision: with different criteria, the same population yields different figures (Wagner et al. 2020). In Spanish, studies with psychometric criteria report between 2% and 12%, depending on the criterion and population (Jiménez et al. 2009; Cubilla-Bonnetier 2024; Cuadro, von Hagen, and Costa Ball 2017; Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011).


Response to instruction
The LEEDUCA early identification guide already proposed assessment at three moments (prediction in preschool, early identification in Grade 1 and diagnosis from Grade 2) as an alternative to “waiting to fail” (Luque 2022). The new definition of the International Dyslexia Association places at its center difficulty that persists despite adequate instruction (International Dyslexia Association 2025; Catts, Haynes, and Joshi 2026). It had already been shown that observing how a child responds to good early intervention separates those with a persistent difficulty from those who had simply had few opportunities (Vellutino et al. 2008). The clinical criteria of the DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association 2022) and ICD-11 (Organización Mundial de la Salud 2019) also require that the difficulty persist and not be explained by other causes. Details are in What we measure in light of the new definition.

title: What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia
text:
The 2025 definition
In October 2025 the International Dyslexia Association (IDA) adopted a new definition of dyslexia (International Dyslexia Association 2025). It is the first major revision since the 2002 definition (Lyon, Shaywitz, and Shaywitz 2003). It was approved by the IDA Board of Directors after a process of almost two years: an 18-member steering committee, a 74-member advisory committee, a special issue of Annals of Dyslexia and more than 3,000 public comments. Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) explain its rationale, component by component, and give guidance for applying it. At almost the same time, an international expert panel reached another consensus definition through the Delphi method (Carroll et al. 2025).
The definition has six blocks:
Compared with the 2002 definition, the idea of what is “unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities”, which led to the IQ discrepancy, disappears. The continuum, the comparison with peers who receive the same instruction and the value of early support come in. “Neurobiological origin” as the single cause also disappears and becomes one of several interacting influences.
IDA and Delphi: agreement on the essentials, with nuances. The Delphi study rated 55 statements with an 80% agreement threshold. Consensus was reached on 42, which were summarized in nine core statements (Carroll et al. 2025). The two definitions agree on the essentials: a difficulty in accurate and fluent word reading and spelling, present across the whole range of intellectual ability, with multiple causes and a central role for phonological processing. They differ in scope. The Delphi definition includes working memory, processing speed, orthographic processing and comorbidities. The IDA definition focuses on language (phonology, morphology, early oral language) and gives more weight to response to instruction, to the orthography of the language and to early identification. According to Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026), these are differences of emphasis and purpose, not disagreements about the nature of dyslexia. The group’s working document reads these changes as a shift from a reactive logic (“wait to fail”) to a proactive one: prevent, screen everyone, identify early and follow each child over time.

title: What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia
text:
What it is and where the difficulty lies. It is a specific learning difficulty in word reading and/or spelling. It affects accuracy, speed or both, and varies with the orthography of the language.
Continuum and persistence. The difficulties occur along a continuum of severity and persist despite instruction that is effective for peers.
Causes. They are complex: combinations of genetic, neurobiological and environmental influences that interact over development.
Cognitive processes. Phonological and morphological difficulties are common but not universal, and early oral language weakness often foreshadows literacy problems.
Secondary consequences. Reading comprehension, less reading experience and, with it, less growth in language, knowledge and written expression. Psychological well-being and employment may also be affected.
Prevention. Identification and targeted instruction matter at any age, but support before and during the first years of schooling is especially effective.

title: What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia
section: What the platform does with each statement
text:
What the platform does with each statement
In practice, the LEEDUCA platform is one way of putting that proactive logic into action: it assesses all pupils in participating schools three times per school year, from age 3, and compares each child with peers of the same age and school term. The table sets each statement of the definition against what the platform and the manual do today, and against what is missing.



Statement of the definition
What the platform or the manual does today
What is missing




Difficulty in word reading
Word and pseudoword lists from age 5 to 11, with accuracy and time; the criterion for persistent difficulty is built from them (How we estimate risk).
—


… and/or in spelling
There is only a letter dictation task (class C) and orthographic decision, which is a reading task.
Word spelling is not measured. This is the most important gap with respect to the new definition: a word and pseudoword dictation task with norms is needed.


Accuracy, speed or both, depending on the orthography
In Spanish, accuracy reaches ceiling early (89–94% of children read all 12 words correctly at ages 7–8) and the differences lie in speed. This is why the manual expresses reading as words correct per minute (reading speed task sheet).
Separate the “slow but accurate” and “slow and inaccurate” profiles in the report.


Continuum of severity
Percentiles instead of categories, five certainty levels and error margins for every score.
Report the probability of persistent difficulty, not only the level (Wagner et al. 2023).


Persists despite instruction that is effective for peers
Persistent difficulty requires being below the cut-off in at least two school years. The reference is children of the same age and school term.
The platform does not know whether instruction was effective. Proposal: also report the child’s position within their classroom and the classroom’s position against the reference. If the whole classroom is low, the problem probably lies in instruction, not in the child. This is the alternative proposed by Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) when a school’s instruction is poor: compare with classmates who receive the same instruction.


Genetic, neurobiological and environmental causes
School SES index, family risk (2010 cohort) and EEG and fNIRS data in subsamples.
Family risk in all cohorts.


Phonological and morphological difficulties, common but not universal
34 phonological skills tasks (11 in class A). Morphology only in oral form and with small samples (classes B and C). No single task is enough for identification: precursors are used to monitor risk, not as a diagnosis.
Written morphology (derivation, inflection) from age 8.


Early oral language foreshadows the difficulties
22 oral language tasks, but only 1 in class A. In our data, oral language adds little to letters, phonological awareness and RAN in predicting reading difficulty.
A good-quality measure of vocabulary and oral comprehension at ages 4–5. The small added value may be due to the measure, not the construct.


Secondary consequences: comprehension, knowledge, writing
Reading comprehension is used as a non-circular validity criterion.
Written expression.


Psychological well-being
Not measured.
A brief measure of reading anxiety and reading self-concept from Grade 2.


Early support is especially effective
Screening from age 3; Preleo as universal instruction in preschool (Preleo).
Separate universal instruction from supplementary intervention in the data.


IQ not required (the discrepancy disappears)
Task sheets do not use nonverbal reasoning for identification.
—

title: What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia
section: What our data say about the definition
text:
What our data say about the definition
Several statements of the definition can be tested with the platform data. These results also feed into the group’s working document:

The continuum shows up in stability. Of the children at or below the 25th percentile at age 6, only half are still there at age 8. Near the cut-off, classification changes a great deal from one school year to the next. This is the argument against relying on a single school year or a single cut-off.
The dual discrepancy (low level and low growth relative to peers) is not very stable in our data (κ = .12). Response to instruction is a necessary criterion, but measured with only two points it carries a lot of error. Three or more measurements and the reliable change threshold are needed (reading speed task sheet).
Precursors are useful for monitoring at age 4 and for screening at age 5. At age 4 the AUC against persistent difficulty is .73; at age 5, .82; with Grade 1 reading, .83–.85.
A modest instrument may be enough. At the end of preschool, letter knowledge alone (AUC .82) predicts practically as well as the combination of phonological awareness, letters and RAN (.82 with cross-cohort validation). A short word list with the cut-off “reads no word” identifies 74% of future cases and raises no alarm for 82% of the children who will not have difficulties.
A transparent orthography shifts the problem to speed, as the definition states. From age 7 the word list no longer discriminates by accuracy, only by time.
Floor effect at the start. At the beginning of learning, children accumulate at the lower end of the distribution (Catts, Haynes, and Joshi 2026). In our data, between 29% and 44% of 5-year-olds read no word or pseudoword. That is why at that age the useful cut-off is “reads none”, not a percentile.
Precursors lose weight once the child can read. For Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026), cognitive correlates are useful for prognosis, not for diagnosis, and explain less unique variance as reading develops. In our data, at age 5 only early reading adds something to letters, phonological awareness and RAN. Oral language, number, memory and executive functions add almost nothing.
The school SES index should neither exclude nor change the cut-off. The definition stresses that an environmental risk does not rule out dyslexia. Our data show that, with the same letter score, children from low-SES schools are at greater risk. Even so, the manual proposes not adjusting the cut-off by SES: the SES-based percentile is given only as context, so that no child who needs support is left without it.

As for the cut-off, the definition does not set one: it leaves the decision to professionals. Some authors speak of one child in five and others of 5–10% (Catts, Haynes, and Joshi 2026). In our cohorts, persistent difficulty affects 15% of children (4% at the strictest level, DL-A, and 11% in DL-B). The five certainty levels make it possible to choose the cut-off according to the intended use.

title: What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia
section: Changes we propose for the manual
text:
Changes we propose for the manual

Theoretical framework (chapter 2 of the outline). Start from the 2025 definition (Catts, Haynes, and Joshi 2026) and the Delphi consensus, with their differences in scope.
Language. Speak of “risk” at ages 4–5, “provisional difficulty” at age 6 and “persistent difficulty” from ages 7–8, as the risk chapter already does. Reserve “dyslexia” for diagnosis, which the platform does not make.
Comparison with peers. Add to the classroom report the child’s position within the classroom and the classroom’s position against the reference.
New tasks for version 1.0: word and pseudoword dictation, a good-quality oral language measure at ages 4–5, written morphology and a brief measure of reading well-being.
Probability instead of a label. Report the probability of persistent difficulty with its interval, consistent with the continuum.

title: The LEEDUCA platform
text:
Chapter map
In one sentence. LEEDUCA is a web platform of the University of Málaga that presents the tasks on the school’s computer, records responses and response times, and organizes the assessment of children aged 3 to 11 in short sessions, three times per school year, to follow reading development and identify early those who fall behind.
The analyses behind these sections are in the group’s internal workspace (restricted access).

title: The LEEDUCA platform
text:
What it was designed for
The platform answers a practical problem: assessing all children in a school, several times per school year, with the resources the school already has. Its design principles, set out in earlier drafts of the manual, are four:

Continuous assessment. Three assessments per school year, in late November, mid-February and late May, to see whether instruction is working and whether each child is progressing like their peers.
Short sessions. Each session lasts 15 minutes at most. Tasks are therefore brief and target a specific skill, which changes from one session to the next: for example, counting syllables in November and matching final syllables in February.
Increasing difficulty. Tasks are ordered by difficulty within and across school years, to avoid ceiling effects and to discriminate among children near the mean, not only those with a clear delay.
Simple administration. Stimulus presentation, recording and scoring are done by the platform. This reduces differences between examiners and allows school staff to administer the assessment after brief training.

Besides assessment, the platform hosts the group’s intervention programs: Preleo (universal, intensification and review) for preschool, and Leetrea, for reading at ages 6 to 8, whose screening is made up of the tasks for ages 6 to 11. This manual deals mainly with assessment; intervention appears where it affects the interpretation of scores (see The Preleo program and The Leetrea program).

title: The LEEDUCA platform
text:
How it is administered
Who assesses. Specialists at each school (speech and language teachers, speech-language therapists) and student trainees, after brief training. Before starting, meetings are held with speech and language teachers and preschool teachers to explain the aims, requirements and procedures.
Whom. All children enrolled in the participating school years, including those with difficulties or who are learning Spanish. To compute task properties and norms, those cases are excluded afterwards (pending: document the exclusion criteria in chapter 4).
How. In most tasks administration is individual: the child sits with the examiner in front of the computer, the platform presents the stimulus and the examiner marks with the mouse whether the response is correct. Of the 63 activities whose configuration has been reviewed on the platform, the examiner responds in 50 and the child in 10. There are three exceptions worth distinguishing when interpreting the data:

Self-administered tasks, in which the child responds with the mouse (for example, the numerical cognition tasks of 2021/22).
Group tasks, such as screening with TECLE or decoding and vocabulary in a multiple-choice format, answered by a whole group at once.
Recorded stimuli, which the child hears through headphones (phoneme and syllable deletion, verbal memory). This way everyone hears the stimulus in the same way, regardless of the examiner’s voice.

title: The LEEDUCA platform
text:
How it is organized
The platform is built on three elements:

Activity. A specific task with its items, instructions and configuration. Each one has a numeric code (e.g., 1931 = reading of two-syllable words). There are more than 12,000 activities, most of them for intervention.
Session. A list of activities administered together. In assessments, each session is a battery for one age and term of a specific school year, with a three-digit code (e.g., 184 = battery for age 7, first term of 2017/18). There are 86 assessment sessions with content, using 464 different activities.
Record. Each time a child completes an activity, a row with their results is saved. This is what is downloaded for analysis.

In this manual each activity is assigned to a canonical task: the same task even if its code changes between cohorts or it has several forms. The master dictionary stores this equivalence, and the Task catalog shows it task by task.

Task types
Activities are built with a small number of presentation engines. The engine determines what the child sees, who responds and what can be measured:

Item-level data are what make possible what this manual adds to the previous ones: internal consistency with ω, item response models, session validity indicators and response time models (see How each task sheet is built).
With these measures, each task is summarized in a main measure according to its family: correct responses in accuracy tasks, stimuli per second in rapid naming, words per minute in reading fluency, and so on. In the manual all of them are presented so that higher is better (see How tasks are grouped).

text:
The DIS-ESP battery
DIS-ESP is the direct antecedent of the platform: many LEEDUCA tasks come from it and keep their project code on the platform. The catalog has 21 DIS-ESP tasks, 6 of them shared with LEEDUCA. Among the DIS-ESP tasks are TECLE, rapid naming of objects on a card and several reading and spelling tasks.
The tests, their rationale, the two-stage procedure and which of them moved to the platform are described in the chapter The DIS-ESP battery (November 8, 2026). Pending (with Marisol Carrillo): what changed in each test when it moved to the platform, and the paper norms that are still available.

title: The LEEDUCA platform
section: Data quality: what you need to know
text:
Data quality: what you need to know
The platform changed format several times, and the data for each cohort were exported and processed at different times. Before using a task, its known issues must be checked. The main ones detected so far are:

Times in a different unit: ×1000 in the old platform (2011 and 2012 cohorts) and in one later session (letters in session 907 of 2014).
Times recorded as zero for some children in some sessions, especially in rapid naming.
Columns copied by mistake in two 2010 sessions (184 and 189) and incomplete sessions in the cohort files.
A wrong answer key in TECLE (five items), still present in the current version of the platform.
Misassigned tasks: the 2021/22 group lexical decision task was confused with list reading.

All of them are listed in the issues sheet of the master dictionary, and each task sheet records its own. The criteria for classifying tasks by the quality of their data are in Limitations and data quality.

title: The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform
text:
Where it comes from
In one sentence. DIS-ESP is a paper battery for assessing dyslexia in two stages (group screening of reading efficiency, then an individual assessment of the reading mechanisms and of phonology), created at the University of Murcia by M. S. Carrillo and J. Alegría. Many of its tests moved, almost unchanged, to the LEEDUCA platform.
The DIS-ESP battery (a battery for assessing specific reading and spelling difficulties) was developed by M. S. Carrillo’s DILEMA research group at the University of Murcia, with J. Alegría (Université Libre de Bruxelles) and other Spanish, Belgian and French researchers. It was created for research and was also designed as a diagnostic instrument for school guidance teams. The LEEDUCA group administered it on paper in Málaga between 2007 and 2012, before moving it to the online platform (see The LEEDUCA platform).
Its two-stage procedure is the direct antecedent of the platform. It was used to study the prevalence of dyslexia in all the schools of a municipality in Murcia (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011) (see Universal screening).
crumbs: 5  The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform

title: The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform
text:
Theoretical basis
The battery starts from four ideas (Carrillo Gallego and Alegría Iscoa 2009):

What is specific to reading is recognizing written words. Understanding a text also requires vocabulary and syntax, but that is not specific to reading: if it is missing, oral comprehension fails too (Gough and Tunmer 1986). Dyslexia is therefore sought in the mechanisms of word identification.
There are two identification mechanisms. The phonological mechanism converts letters into sounds and shows in pseudoword reading. The orthographic mechanism recognizes the word by its written form, stored in the orthographic lexicon. Spanish has no irregular words with which to measure it, so the battery assesses it with words containing inconsistent spellings (b/v, g/j, h): deciding which of two forms is correctly spelled, or writing it to dictation, is only possible if its written form has been stored.
The engine of learning is phonological. Learning to read requires becoming aware of the phonological structure of the language. Syllabic awareness precedes reading and phonemic awareness develops with it; according to longitudinal and training studies, its relation with reading is causal.
Phonology has several dimensions. Besides phonological awareness, speech sound discrimination, access to and retrieval of the phonological representations of words, and working memory all count. Their deficits are not specific to reading and are usually mild in everyday speech, but they can explain why a child does not learn to read.

title: The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform
text:
The two-stage procedure
First stage: group screening. The whole class takes the reading efficiency test. In the validation study a double criterion was used so as not to confuse dyslexia with school conditions: the child had to be below the mean minus 1 SD of their class and grade in their school, and also below the mean minus 1 SD of all children in their grade (Carrillo Gallego and Alegría Iscoa 2009). In the prevalence study, the cut-off was the mean minus 1.5 SD (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011).
Second stage: individual assessment. The flagged children take the rest of the tests, which look for the proximal cause of the problem: which identification mechanism fails (phonological, orthographic or both) and which aspect of phonology is affected.
The diagnostic module. The battery compares each result with two reference groups:

By chronological age: children of the same age (in the practice norms, age 9).
By reading level: younger children who read at the same level (in the practice norms, age 7).

A deficit that appears relative to children of the same age but not relative to those of the same reading level indicates a delay; one that also appears relative to those of the same reading level indicates different functioning. With this comparison, the module proposes a profile (phonological, surface or mixed). Later research has shown that subtypes depend heavily on the comparison group, and that far fewer appear with reading-level controls (Carrillo Gallego, Alegría, and Calvo Rodríguez 2008; Sprenger-Charolles 2011) (see Theoretical framework).
crumbs: 5  The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform

title: The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform
text:
What its validation showed
The validation study included 71 schoolchildren with specific reading delay and 80 typical readers from the same classrooms, in Grades 2 to 6 (Carrillo Gallego and Alegría Iscoa 2009):

Children with dyslexia performed worse on all tests, both the reading and spelling tests and all the phonological ones.
The delay in reading and spelling grows across grades. Children with dyslexia did not reach the reading efficiency of Grade 2 typical readers until Grade 5 or 6.
Slow and inaccurate at the same time. In words and pseudowords, the slowest were also those who made the most errors. That is why the battery proposed a single index: correct responses per second. The platform uses efficiency measures of the same kind.
Naming reveals an access problem. Repetition of the pictures helped children with dyslexia more and name length hurt them more, which points to difficulties in retrieving and producing phonological forms.
Verbal fluency depended on naming. When naming speed was controlled, the difference in fluency disappeared.
crumbs: 5  The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform

title: The DIS-ESP battery: the paper origin of the platform
text:
Use of the paper tests
The group has decided that the DIS-ESP paper tests will be free to use. Before publishing them here, the final version of each booklet and how to cite it must be confirmed with their author. TECLE is not included: it is a published test and is cited, but not reproduced.
The battery was also administered in Colombia, with TECLE in 3 minutes instead of 5. Those results will be incorporated in a later version.

The map shows two different designs within the same database:

Term-by-term follow-up (to 2019/20). Three assessments per school year from age 4 (2011–2015 cohorts) or age 5 (2010 cohort), with between 300 and 950 children per time point and gradual attrition with age.
Broad assessments of 2020/21 and 2021/22 (orange border). A single assessment per year, in February, with many new children. After the pandemic began, paper versions were administered, mainly of efficiency tests, from Grade 2 to Grade 6 (tabulated data in 03_PAPEL_TABLETS_PANDEMIA; the TECLE, PEALE and syntax booklets are in the folder of the Colombia project). They are two different batteries (Table 6.3):

School year 2021/22, with about 260–470 children per cohort: text comprehension, Woodcock, lexical decision, homographs, reading comprehension, reading speed and mathematics (and, in the 2014 and 2015 cohorts, phoneme segmentation and initial letter).


Paper or platform? The structure of the output settles this (cap4_estructura_sesiones_v1.R). The 2021 assessment (session 2021) only contains the number of responses, correct responses and errors per test, with no times: it is the tabulation of the paper booklets. text:
Decisions and pending issues

Preleo condition (decided November 2, 2026). The preferred source is the information from Auxiliadora Sánchez: in the 2010 cohort, the classification in her thesis (19 schools with Preleo and 11 without it, with implementation fidelity); in the 2011 cohort, all children are Preleo. Implemented in assignment v5. Also decided (November 2, 2026): the condition applies only to children in the term-by-term follow-up; for those who appear only in the broad assessments it stays “unknown”, because their schools are not in the Preleo follow-up for their cohort (assignment v6, asignar_preleo_v6.R; the table in 4.4 already uses it). The 2012 cohort and the 2013 and 2014 exceptions also need to be checked with A. Sánchez.
School names (done). Version v5 uses the v2 matching (by similarity and with manual checking) as the canonical school: 65–72 schools in the large cohorts and 31 in the small ones, compared with 79–96 names on the platform. Between 209 and 346 children per cohort remain without a matched school, mostly from schools that appear only in the broad assessments.
2020/21 and 2021/22 assessments (done). 2021: TECLE battery on paper, with no times. 2021/22: platform on tablets, with a time limit. It remains to decide whether separate norms will be built and how they are cited in articles that use reading at age 8 or older.

title: Psychometric method
text:
Chapter map
In one sentence. Each task is analyzed with the method that fits the way it measures (not all with α), each score is reported with its margin of error, and each use the manual proposes (screening, monitoring, identification) rests on specific evidence (American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, and National Council on Measurement in Education 2014; Kane 2013).
The analyses behind these sections are in the group’s internal workspace (restricted access).

Section

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.1 Scores
One main measure per task, according to its family. Tasks are grouped into seven families according to how they measure: accuracy, rapid naming, oral reading fluency, time-limited efficiency, decision with response time, span and memory, and comprehension. The family determines the main measure, its transformation and the reliability method (see How tasks are grouped).
Higher is better. In the manual all scores are presented so that a high value is good and a low percentile indicates difficulty. Times are converted into rates (stimuli per second, words per minute).
Understandable units. Where possible, the score is also given in a unit a teacher understands: words per minute, minutes to read 1,000 words, or “reads like a child of…” (see Norms by reading level).
Session validity. Item-level times make it possible to detect an anomalous administration: times of zero, different units, interruptions, responses that are too fast, or results inconsistent with the same child at other time points. A first set of rules fixed in advance has been tested on the rapid naming tasks. The proposal is that each score carry a reliable session or check flag.

Missing: extend the detectors to all tasks and decide the thresholds.

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.2 Reliability
The method depends on the family. Internal consistency (α, ω) only makes sense in accuracy tasks without a time limit. In speeded tasks α overestimates reliability, and test–retest or parallel forms are appropriate.








Family
Main reliability
Complement




Accuracy, comprehension, span
ω (or KR-20) from item responses
Test–retest; IRT and conditional standard error


Rapid naming, reading fluency
Test–retest and parallel forms
Reliability across cards or lists


Time-limited, decision
Test–retest; split-half by time
Joint model of speed and accuracy



What is available today. Of the 110 assessment tasks in the catalog, 55 have a 2021 α and 33 have stability across successive administrations (ρ); 64 have at least one of the two and 46 have no reliability data yet. Stability mixes measurement error and real change, so it is a lower bound.
Standard error and bands. Each percentile comes with its 90% confidence band, computed with the standard error of measurement. With IRT, the error is conditional: wider at the extremes, where risk decisions are made.
What a reliability of .85 implies. A child whose true level is at P20 may appear not at risk in about 4 of every 10 assessments. The interactive simulation is in The dancing percentile (in Spanish). That is why reports use a watch zone between P20 and P30, in which no label is given until the next assessment (see The watch zone (in Spanish)).

Missing: ω and IRT with the item-level responses of the new platform for all class A and B tasks; short-term test–retest in the speeded tasks. This is what could change the most quality classes.

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.3 Validity



Source of evidence
What is done
Status




Content
Description of the task, items and instructions read from the platform; brief theoretical framework per task
In the pilot task sheets and in 18 frameworks by domain


Internal structure
Factors (precursors, decoding, fluency, comprehension) and networks by age
Exploratory networks by age; confirmatory factor analysis missing

By sex, format (platform, paper, tablet), period and region

Convergent and external criterion

Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (see Validity against the Woodcock-Muñoz battery)


Predictive and diagnostic

Done with cross-cohort validation (see How we estimate risk)

Pending



The criterion. Reading difficulty is defined with the child’s whole trajectory from age 6 to 11, in certainty levels (persistent, transient, typical…), not with a single assessment. This makes the criterion more stable and reduces spectrum bias. When the criterion contains the task itself, the AUC is presented only as agreement, not as predictive validity.
Beyond the cut-off. The manual proposes giving probabilities and not only a cut-off: likelihood ratios by score band and posterior probability according to the school’s prevalence. The first analyses show that a well-calibrated Bayesian model outperforms the single cut-off, and that multiplying likelihood ratios overestimates risk when indicators are correlated.

Missing: confirmatory factor analysis by age, invariance by sex and format, and group agreement on the certainty levels and the threshold for severe difficulty (P10 vs. −1.5 SD).

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.4 Norms
The reference sample. Norms describe development without intervention: the reference is the children from schools that did not implement Preleo with their cohort. All equivalent cohorts are pooled, unless one departs by more than 1 SD (see Methodological decisions).
By time point, not only by school year. With three assessments per school year, a single norm per school year flags almost a quarter of the children as “at risk” in the first term. That is why norms are built by school year and term, and from age 4 to 6 they are refined by age in months (see Norms by school year or by term).
Continuous norms. The aim is to replace the empirical tables with continuous norms by age (cNORM or GAMLSS), which smooth the percentiles, allow norming at any exact age and use all cohorts at once.

Missing: continuous norms for class A tasks, separate tables for Preleo schools, and norms for age 3 and for the versions in other languages.

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.5 How much change matters
In a monitoring system, the key question is not only where a child stands, but whether they have really progressed and whether that progress matters. The manual answers with three complementary indicators:

Reliable change index: whether the difference between two assessments exceeds what is expected from measurement error. Already in the letters and speed task sheets.
Growth percentile: how much a child has progressed compared with those who started at the same level.
Minimal important change: how much change matters, anchored in external criteria (reading prognosis, teacher judgment, the shift from transient to persistent difficulty) (Anvari and Lakens 2021).

Beware of regression to the mean. Among children flagged as at risk, some “leave” risk at the next assessment purely because of measurement error: with a reliability of .85, more than one in four without having changed (see Leaving risk is not always improving (in Spanish)). That is why leaving risk is confirmed with another assessment.

Missing: settle the anchors and apply the three indicators to the class A reading tasks.

title: Psychometric method
text:
5.6 Fairness
A fair task measures the same thing and makes the same errors in all groups. This is checked in two ways: differential functioning of items and scores (sex, school socioeconomic status, format, region) and differential prediction, that is, whether the same cut-off is equally accurate in all groups. The letters task sheet has already shown that, at the same score, children from low-SES schools are at greater risk; for that reason the cut-off is not adjusted for socioeconomic status.

Missing: false-positive rates by group in the screening tasks.

title: Psychometric method
text:
Reproducibility
All computations are done with R scripts on the project’s computer, which read the complete data and export only aggregated tables. The book is built from those tables, and the code is in the repository. Before confirmatory studies, the analysis plan is preregistered (see How each task sheet is built).

title: How each task sheet is built
text:
Sections of a task sheet
Task sheets follow the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, and National Council on Measurement in Education 2014) and the argument-based approach to validity (Kane 2013): each use proposed for a score (identifying risk, monitoring progress, comparing with norms) must be backed by specific evidence.

title: How each task sheet is built
text:
What backs each proposal
When a task sheet proposes a use or a decision, it states what it rests on:

[E] Published evidence: peer-reviewed studies that support the measure or the criterion.
[D] Our own data: analyses of the LEEDUCA data shown in the task sheet.
[U] Utility criterion: a proposal by the group based on its clinical, educational or research value, still without direct evidence.
crumbs: 8  How each task sheet is built

title: How each task sheet is built
text:
Reference sample and Preleo
Preleo is a prevention program that some schools delivered in preschool. So that the norms describe development without intervention, the main reference is the normative reference sample: children from schools that did not deliver Preleo to their cohort. In analyses of the program’s effect, the terms Preleo group and comparison group are used. “Control group” is not used because schools were not randomly assigned. Tables show the internal codes SIN (non-Preleo) and CON (Preleo).
crumbs: 8  How each task sheet is built

title: How each task sheet is built
text:
The innovations
Besides the classical indicators, task sheets include analyses designed for the real use of the platform:

Agreement between terms and reliable change: how much a child has to change to claim that they have really improved.
Precision of the percentile: the band within which a child’s percentile lies with 90% confidence.
Age in months: whether it is better to norm by exact age and not only by school year and term (see Norms by school year or by term).
Validity without circularity: when the reading difficulty criterion contains the measure itself, another criterion is sought.
Differential prediction: whether the same cut-off works equally well for boys and girls or for schools of different socioeconomic status.
Understandable units: for example, words per minute and the minutes a child takes to read 1,000 words.

Reproducibility
Computation is done in two layers. On the project’s computer, R scripts read the complete data and produce aggregated tables. The script analisis/exportar_agregados.R transfers those tables to the book and checks that none of them identifies a child, a teacher or a school. The book is built only from those tables.

title: How tasks are grouped
text:
Task sheet families
The platform’s tasks can be grouped in two ways, and the manual needs both:
A rule common to all families: in the manual, every score is presented so that higher is better, and a low percentile always indicates difficulty. That way there is no need to remember that in rapid naming a long time is bad, or that in a decision task a short time is good. The original direction is kept in the data, and the task sheet states it.
What is measured and what is reported
How each family is analyzed
Each task’s family appears in the Task catalog, where tasks can also be filtered by family.
From the family to the automatic task sheet. Each family fixes the parameters of its task sheet: main measure, direction, transformation, reliability method, type of norms, figures and caveats. With that, generating a new task sheet only requires three things:
The five pilot task sheets were made almost this way. The next step is to turn the draft task sheet script into a common one for all families.
