What it shows:

Rapid naming is a factor of its own at all ages. The object versions load together (.74–.88 from age 4 to 6; .37–.88 at ages 7 and 8) and separately from phonological awareness, as the double-deficit hypothesis predicts. The color version separates at age 4: another reason to review it (see the warning in the catalog).
At age 4, the syllabic tasks (matching and deleting syllables) form a factor. Oral language (morphology, comprehension, vocabulary) forms another, and speech perception and visual-attentional span, two more.
At age 5 an early reading factor already appears: letters, initial letter, syllables and first words, together with phoneme segmentation and deletion. Phonemic awareness joins letter knowledge. A counting factor and a reasoning factor (Raven) also separate out.
At age 6, decoding is a single, very strong factor: syllables, words, pseudowords and text speed, with loadings from .63 to .86. Phonemic awareness (blending, identification) remains in a separate factor.
At age 7 reading begins to differentiate. Words, pseudowords and TECLE remain in one factor, and text speed forms another with orthographic decision.
At age 8 words (with TECLE) and pseudowords are already separate factors. Phonological awareness and verbal memory remain together.
Text comprehension does not form a factor of its own. It shares a factor with calculation at age 7 and with phonological awareness at age 8, with moderate loadings (.39–.45).

Implications for the manual:

Composite scores by age should follow these factors: rapid naming, phonological awareness (syllabic at age 4 and phonemic from age 5), decoding, text fluency and oral language.
Reading comprehension is not just “more decoding”: it needs its own validity criterion.
Tasks with low loadings on all factors are candidates for review or for moving to appendix D: some visual-attentional, speech perception and attention tasks.

Caveats. This is an exploratory analysis with pairwise correlations across different cohorts. At age 6 the fit is worse and there is a loading of 1.00 (reading comprehension), a sign that this task overlaps almost entirely with another. What is needed now is a confirmatory analysis by cohort, with the same children on all tasks, and a test of invariance across ages and cohorts.

title: How tasks are grouped
text:
Task networks
Factor analysis assumes that behind the tasks there are a few latent skills. Network analysis starts from a different idea: skills support one another and form a system. What is estimated is the network of partial correlations between tasks, that is, how much two tasks are related after removing all the others. Technically it is a regularized Gaussian graphical model (EBICglasso). The network’s groupings (communities) can be compared with the factors, as in exploratory graph analysis (EGA).

What the network adds to the factors:

Communities largely coincide with the factors (ARI from 0.45 to 0.73). That two methods with different assumptions reach similar groupings gives more confidence in them.
The network becomes denser with age. Density goes from 0.19 at age 4 to 0.88 at age 8: skills become integrated as children learn to read. This is what the mutualism model of cognitive development predicts.
Rapid naming is a community of its own at all ages. At ages 4 and 5 it connects to the rest of the network through phonological awareness and oral language. From age 6 it connects almost only to reading, and barely to phonological awareness. This is to be expected if rapid naming is related mainly to reading fluency.
Bridge tasks. Some tasks connect different communities: at age 5, phoneme identification and deletion; at age 6, letter knowledge and phoneme deletion. They are natural candidates for composite scores and for intervention.
Strong negative edges (for example, between the two readings of the same text at age 6) indicate nearly redundant tasks or overlapping measures. It is a signal for review, not a real relation.

Caveats. Like the factor analysis, it combines cohorts pairwise, so it is exploratory. The stability of the edges still needs to be checked (bootstrap) with child-level data. That analysis and longitudinal network models (how the network changes from one school year to the next) are a methodological study in their own right: see the Research agenda (in Spanish).

Rapid naming, which is key in the risk model, does not yet reach class A in any of its forms: it does not lack quality, it lacks the data to check it (it has no α, and the same form is rarely repeated with the same children).
One class A task needs revision before use: inhibition has a very high α, but its measure is on hold until the way it is scored is reviewed. Classes are computed with automatic rules, and the group can correct them.
Available reliability is uneven. Several class A tasks rely only on stability or only on the 2021 α. Computing ω from the item responses of the new platform will complete the column (see Psychometric method).

What it shows:

Reading fluency is the most stable measure within the school year: between terms (≤ 4 months) its median stability is around .76, compared with .51 for accuracy tasks, and it stays above .60 up to 12 months. This is consistent with reading speed being the best indicator for monitoring in a transparent orthography.
Beyond one year, stability drops in all families. Part of this is real change, and part is that the “same” task changes its list or text between school years. This must be checked before interpreting long-term stability.
Preschool accuracy tasks are less stable, partly because of ceiling effects and few items, and partly because children change a lot at those ages. The dotted lines mark the traffic-light thresholds (.40 and .60).
Stability of the difficulty label is high in the first school years and lower later. Of the children below the 10th percentile at age 6, 89% are still below the 25th at age 7; starting from the 25th percentile, 78%. From age 7 to 8 these figures drop to 66% and 51%. That is why the manual defines difficulty using the whole trajectory and not a single assessment (see How we estimate risk).

What they show. From age 6, the model with the expected factors fits clearly better than a general factor (at age 6, CFI .94 vs. .84; at ages 7 and 8, .93–.94 vs. .77–.80), with an RMSEA that is still somewhat high (.09–.10) and should improve when comprehension and other tasks are added. The most interesting result is the relation between accuracy and fluency. At ages 5 and 6 their factors correlate .98 and .94: they are practically the same skill, because reading accurately and reading quickly still go together. At ages 7 and 8 the correlation drops to .75 and .74, and separating them improves fit considerably (CFI .93 vs. .80 if merged). Once most children read accurately, the differences between them lie in automatization. Phonological awareness also becomes less tied to reading with age (with accuracy, from .82 at age 6 to .66–.69 at ages 7–8; with fluency, from .75 to .56).

title: How we estimate risk and reading difficulty
text:
Reading in each school year
A single low score in one term is not enough to speak of reading difficulty. A child may have a bad day, have just arrived, or progress at a different pace and later catch up with their peers. That is why the manual distinguishes between risk, which is estimated before children read, and difficulty, which is only confirmed when reading remains low over several school years.
Two ideas from the literature support this approach:
From age 6, reading in each school year combines two components:
Each component is expressed as a percentile against the normative reference sample: children from non-Preleo schools in all cohorts (2010–2013). Reading for the school year is the mean of the two.
Cohorts are pooled because they are equivalent: for the same task and time point, the median difference between a cohort and the pooled reference is d = 0.11. If a cohort departs by more than 1 SD from the others, or its spread is more than three times larger or smaller (a change in task version or an export error), it uses its own reference, and this is recorded.

title: How we estimate risk and reading difficulty
text:
Five certainty levels
Using reading in the school years from age 6 to 11, each child is assigned one of five levels. At least two school years must have been assessed, one of them from age 7 onward.








Level
What it means
Rule




DL-A · Severe persistent reading difficulty
Reading stays very low year after year
≤ P10 in at least two school years and ≤ P25 in all years from age 7


DL-B · Persistent reading difficulty
Reading stays low in most school years
≤ P25 in at least two school years and in at least half of them


TR · Transient difficulty
Low in some school year, but not sustained
≤ P25 in some school year


INT · Intermediate
Never low, but in the lower part of the average
Never ≤ P25 and mean percentile < 40


TE · Stable typical
Reading at or above the average in all school years
Never ≤ P25 and mean percentile ≥ 40



DL-A and DL-B together make up persistent difficulty: the criterion against which the predictive validity of the tasks is studied. DL-A versus TE makes up the certainty sample, with the clearest cases at both extremes. It is used to check whether a task discriminates well when there is no doubt about the classification.

title: How we estimate risk and reading difficulty
text:
How well the precursors predict
With the precursors at age 5 (phonological awareness, letters and rapid naming), persistent difficulty is predicted with an area under the curve of .82, validated by leaving each cohort out. At age 4 it is .73, and with both school years together, .83. Letters and phonological awareness carry most of the weight; rapid naming adds nothing at age 5.
At age 4 the precursors are useful for monitoring, not for screening. At age 5 they already allow support to be prioritized, always as risk and not as a diagnosis. Details are in each task sheet and in a prediction article in preparation.

section: Universal screening: what the evidence says and where the platform fits
text:
Universal screening: what the evidence says and where the platform fits

How many children: prevalence depends on the criterion
Figures for dyslexia in Spanish vary widely, and the main reason is the criterion used to identify it:









Source
Population
Criterion
Prevalence




Meta-analysis in Spanish (Cubilla-Bonnetier 2024)

Grade 2 to Year 10
Text comprehension
20.2% with comprehension problems; 6.7% poor comprehenders



Four takeaways for the manual:

There is no single “true” prevalence. Reading is continuously distributed, so the figure depends on the cut-off (Wagner et al. 2020). That is why the platform does not report a prevalence, but certainty levels with their percentage in each cohort.
With psychometric criteria, the figure in primary school is around 9–12%. This is what results from a first group stage and an individual confirmation (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011; Jiménez et al. 2009).
Schools identify late and too little. Andalusia’s 1.24%, diagnosed at around age 10, against an expected 5–8%, points to underdiagnosis. Identification in preschool and Grade 1 is exactly what the platform can contribute.
Comprehension is a different problem. A substantial share of poor comprehenders have no decoding difficulty. This is the reason for adding comprehension as a separate dimension (see “Pending”).



The precedent: DIS-ESP’s two-stage screening
The Molina de Segura study (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011) is the platform’s direct antecedent. M. S. Carrillo and J. Alegría, authors of the DIS-ESP battery, applied a sequential procedure to all primary school children in one municipality:

First stage. Group TECLE in the classroom. The cut-off (mean − 1.5 SD of typical readers) is equivalent to a delay of about two school years. It flagged 12.5% of the children, compared with the 6.7% that would be expected if reading were normally distributed. This indicates that the distribution has a heavier lower tail, where readers with dyslexia are concentrated.
Second stage. Word and pseudoword reading and spelling tests (dictation of words with inconsistent spellings and orthographic decision) to look for the proximal cause. Of the flagged children, 96% had a deficit in the phonological mechanism, the orthographic one or both. 77% had both.

Three results from that study reappear in the platform data:

Delay in Grade 2 is partly transient. In Grade 2, 18% of delayed readers had only an orthographic problem (5% in Grade 6), and a quarter read pseudowords well. The authors expected many of them to recover with more practice. This is what the platform captures with the TR level (transient difficulty) as opposed to DL-A and DL-B.
Around 10% keep the difficulty in Grades 4 and 6, many without reaching even a Grade 2 reading level.
Figures depend on the procedure. With the same approach, 8.6% was found in the Canary Islands (Jiménez et al. 2009), but the first selection was made by teachers (27.9% of the sample) and the cut-off was the bottom 25% on PROLEC.

The platform turns that procedure into a continuous one: the first stage is repeated three times per school year from age 3, and the second (words, pseudowords, orthographic decision) is already in the same battery.


What accuracy to expect from screening

In Spanish there are screeners with good accuracy in preschool. A set of curriculum-based measures in the final year of preschool reached an AUC of .83 in autumn and of .94–.97 in winter and spring. Phonemic awareness and knowledge of letter–sound correspondences were the best single measures (Gutiérrez et al. 2020). Lexiland, a tablet-based screener for 5-year-olds, identified 90% of those who would have difficulties at the end of Grade 1, with a specificity of 76% (Zugarramurdi et al. 2022). In Catalan, Prelectocat provides cut-offs at age 5 (López-Sala et al. 2025).
Sensitivity tends to fall short. A meta-analysis of 30 studies of computer-adaptive screeners finds a specificity of .83 and a sensitivity of .77, below the .80 recommended for universal screening (Shen et al. 2026). Cut-offs computed with local data improve sensitivity at the cost of specificity.
Repeating or adding a second stage reduces false positives. Adding brief progress monitoring or a dynamic assessment reduced false positives in Grade 1 (Compton et al. 2010). A second stage only with children who do not pass the first increases specificity, but may lower sensitivity (Klingbeil et al. 2017). It works better if the second measure adds information different from the first: two highly correlated measures barely reduce false positives (Van Norman et al. 2019).



The LEEDUCA early identification guide
The group’s guide for speech and language teachers and preschool and primary teachers (Luque 2022) organizes assessment in three moments, each with its own aim:

Prediction or risk assessment, in preschool, before formal reading instruction.
Early identification, in the first year of learning to read (Grade 1), with at least three assessments of all children, because a single measurement is not enough.
Psychoeducational assessment and diagnosis, from Grade 2, instead of “waiting to fail”.

To assess risk, it proposes four criteria, each with a judgment of mild, moderate or severe risk: family risk (with a case history and the ATLAS questionnaire), oral language (first the phonological triad: phonological awareness, rapid naming and verbal memory; then the semantic, grammatical and prosodic components), visual hypotheses and comorbidity with other neurodevelopmental disorders (DLD, ADHD, dyscalculia and developmental coordination disorder). For early identification, direct assessment of reading (phonological route, visual route, speed and comprehension) takes precedence as the criterion for intensifying instruction, even if the other criteria do not confirm the risk, and it is graded with cut-offs at P10, P20 and P30.
The platform and this manual follow that logic: universal and repeated assessment, several indicators rather than one, direct reading as the main criterion from Grade 1, and graded judgments (see Report bands). What the manual adds is estimation with data: calibrated probabilities, certainty levels and a watch zone.


Where the platform fits

Comparable accuracy. The age-5 model (AUC .82, validated by leaving each cohort out) is within the range of published screeners in Spanish.
Monitoring is already built in. Three assessments per school year are equivalent to the second stage or the progress monitoring recommended in the literature. No published screener in Spanish has that monitoring at this scale.
A two-gate procedure. The scheme and its rationale are in The two-gate funnel (in Spanish).
Proposed study. Use the platform data to simulate two-stage screening: a first stage with letters and phonological awareness, and a second with the least correlated task (for example, RAN or change between terms). Compute sensitivity and specificity against persistent difficulty and against Woodcock-Muñoz.

title: How we estimate risk and reading difficulty
section: Why this variable is useful in other analyses
text:
Why this variable is useful in other analyses
The certainty level summarizes a child’s whole reading trajectory in a single variable, built with fixed rules and the same reference for all cohorts. It can therefore also serve as an outcome in other studies; for example, to compare the proportion of persistent difficulty between schools with and without a program, or to describe which severity group children with a given risk profile end up in.
Caution: the level is built from words, pseudowords and text speed. Comparing those same tasks against it from age 6 is therefore circular: it measures agreement, not predictive validity (see the reading speed task sheet).
crumbs: 12  How we estimate risk and reading difficulty

title: How we estimate risk and reading difficulty
text:
Why this classification
Group decision (November 8, 2026). The manual adopts the five certainty levels as the reference classification of reading difficulty, with P10 as the threshold for severe difficulty (DL-A), instead of −1.5 SD (≈ P7). Three reasons:

It uses the trajectory, not a snapshot. Difficulty is defined over several school years, as the IDA definition requires by placing at its center difficulty that persists despite instruction (International Dyslexia Association 2025). A single assessment is not enough.
It separates certainty from severity. Distinguishing severe persistent (DL-A), persistent (DL-B) and transient (TR) difficulty makes it possible to study what distinguishes children who recover from those who do not, which is a central theoretical question for cumulative risk and resilience models (Catts and Petscher 2022).
It is less conservative without losing certainty. With P10, fewer children with severe difficulty go unidentified, and the requirement that it be repeated in at least two school years and not exceed P25 from age 7 preserves certainty.

The same logic for oral language and mathematics (proposal)
The classification does not depend on reading: it only requires one measure per school year, a cut-off and several assessed school years. The proposal is to apply it in the same way to two other domains:



Domain
Measure per school year (proposed)
First school years with data
Purpose




Oral language
Vocabulary and grammatical comprehension (see Screening two risks)
Ages 4–5
Distinguish weak oral language that persists from weak oral language that recovers; separate the risk of dyslexia from that of language disorder


Mathematics
Arithmetic and magnitude tasks in each school year (see Numerical cognition)
Ages 5–8
Persistent difficulty in mathematics and its co-occurrence with reading difficulty



For the levels to be comparable across domains, the same rules are used (P10 and P25, at least two school years, one from age 7). What must be checked in each domain is that there are enough measures in each school year and that they are reliable.

Missing: compute the oral language and mathematics labels with the same script as the reading labels, and review which tasks enter each school year.

title: Norms by reading level
text:
What it is for
In a dyslexia assessment, each test is interpreted twice. Against chronological age, the child is compared with children of the same age: this documents the difficulty. Against reading level, the child is compared with younger children who read at the same level. This distinguishes a delay (the child progresses more slowly, but like a younger reader of the same level) from a deviance (the child fails even compared with younger readers of the same level). Deviance indicates greater severity.
This second comparison can almost never be made properly, because it requires norms from younger children measured with the same test. The platform has them: it measures the same tasks in the same children from the final year of preschool to Grade 3, three times per school year. This chapter offers two tools:
All scores are correct responses per minute, with the non-Preleo group as reference.

title: Norms by reading level
text:
Caveats

Time points combine different cohorts. From age 7 onward, the reference is mainly the 2010 cohort.
Measurement error. The score used as reading level also has error. A child who scores low by chance on the reference task is compared with a lower level than their real one. With a single reference task, classification near the cut-off is unstable. It is advisable to confirm a deviance at two time points.
Cleaning. The 2021/22 sessions (948–950, to be reviewed) and values above P99 + 3 SD for their time point were excluded. Groups whose median does not fit with that of neighboring time points were also excluded: 2 groups, the two from the 2011 cohort at 8.2. There, the median for three-syllable words is very low (5.0 correct per minute, compared with about 46 at neighboring time points) and that for three-syllable pseudowords is very high (50.4, compared with about 22). This is session 905 (2019/20), which already had anomalous times in EDICOLE. In it, code 1932 (three-syllable words) records 23 correct, 13 errors and almost 5 minutes as medians: it cannot be a list of 12 words. Code 1935 (pseudowords), on the other hand, has the profile of a word list. The codes are probably swapped or misassigned in that session (new data issue; to be reviewed with the engineer and, meanwhile, session 905 should not be used for these tasks).
Text speed. Left out: it mixes versions with different scales. Its norms in words per minute are in the reading speed task sheet.

title: Norms by reading level
section: How to use it in the DIS-ESP summary chart
text:
How to use it in the DIS-ESP summary chart

In the row “Deviation criterion: reading level”, take as the reading level the child’s score on two-syllable words (or, for the visual route, on pseudowords).
Look up the P16 for that level in the table for the corresponding pair. If the other task falls below it, it is a deviance (✗); if not, the mechanism works as in readers of the same level (✓).
If the declared cut-off is different (for example, P10), use that column.

title: Validity against an external criterion: Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency
text:
What it is and why it matters
In the 2021/22 school year, the platform included the reading fluency subtest of the Batería III Woodcock-Muñoz (Muñoz-Sandoval et al. 2005). The child silently reads simple sentences and decides whether they are true or false (for example, “my mother eats buses”), with a 3-minute limit. The score is correct minus errors.
The test was given at the same time to all six cohorts, from age 6 to 11 (2,183 children), in group administration on tablets because of pandemic restrictions (Loredo et al. 2025). It is the best external criterion available to the manual, for three reasons:
“Low reading fluency” means being one standard deviation or more below the mean for one’s age in our sample (around P16).

title: Validity against an external criterion: Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency
text:
Concurrent validity in 2021/22
In the same 2021/22 sessions, lexical decision tasks (“is this a word?”) and sentence comprehension with homographs tasks were also given on tablets. Their relation with Woodcock-Muñoz fluency is high (AUC up to .82 for homographs at ages 10–11). This clarifies an earlier data issue: the “too low” 2021/22 scores in word reading were not an error. They were a different task, group lexical decision, which the dictionary had wrongly assigned to reading lists aloud. It has been corrected (correcciones_tarea_canonica_v2.csv).

title: Validity against an external criterion: Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency
text:
Caveats

Group administration on tablets, during the pandemic, without an external examiner in most schools. The reliability of the original version is high (.90), but it has not been checked in this administration.
A single measurement per child.
Sample loss. At ages 10–11 fewer children remain from the 2010 and 2011 cohorts, and not at random: those who changed school drop out of the follow-up.
No published norms. The distributions by age are in an internal sheet (P_Woodcock_NO_PUBLICAR), for the group’s use only.

text:
What changes in the manual

The validity of the reading task sheets will have, in addition to later comprehension, this non-circular external criterion. It still needs to be added to the automatic task sheet.
The persistent difficulty label now has external validity evidence, which should be cited in articles L2 and L3.
For the 2021/22 lexical decision and homograph tasks, this chapter is the only source of validity. They have a single session and do not enter class A.

title: Limitations and data quality
text:
Starting point
The platform was not born with a measurement plan. Tasks were created, changed and withdrawn according to the needs of each school year. Measuring was preferred over not measuring, and that is enormously valuable: there is longitudinal follow-up of thousands of children from age 4, three times per school year. In exchange, there are problems that cannot be fixed afterwards and others that can. This chapter separates them and says what has been done about each.

title: Limitations and data quality
section: What limits the data and what has been done
text:
What limits the data and what has been done









Problem
Why it matters
What has been done
What is missing




Different batteries by cohort. Each cohort did different tasks at different time points (126 tasks with 207 codes).
Differences between tasks are confounded with differences between cohorts.
Standardization within cohort and session; equivalence between cohorts before pooling for norms; pairwise analyses.
Formal equating between versions and cohorts.


Many versions of the same task. Changes in items, timing or format under the same name.
A score does not mean the same in two sessions.
Master dictionary with canonical tasks; warnings in the catalog when stability is implausible.
Record each version with its date and items.


Few items and ceiling effects in many precursors.
Low reliability at the extremes, exactly where decisions are made.
Reliability by task and quality traffic light; preference for school-year scores, which average terms.
Item response theory to see where each task measures well.


How time is recorded. It is the time of the last response, not the duration; some times were multiplied by 1,000.
Speed measures may confuse slowness with giving up.
Correction of ×1,000 times; plausible-time filters; time is not prorated.
Record start, end and time per item in all tasks.


Scoring by the examiner (correct or incorrect with the mouse) in reading and rapid naming.
Examiner error is part of the score, and it has never been measured.
—
Double scoring in a subsample (recordings) to estimate inter-rater agreement.


Unverified answer keys. TECLE has five items with a wrongly recorded key.
Systematic errors invisible in the totals.
Item-by-item check against the option chosen; rescoring.
An automatic key check for all choice tasks.


Manual matrices with columns shifted by spreadsheet lookups and incomplete sessions.
Published results that may not be reproducible.
Single long table; verification against the raw exports; audit of the Preleo data.
Every new analysis comes from the long table.


Non-random assignment of Preleo, by school, with uneven fidelity.
The effect of the program is confounded with school and socioeconomic status.
Multilevel models, baselines, analysis plan fixed before seeing results.
Acknowledge that it is a quasi-experimental design and say so.


Sample of volunteer schools in Málaga, with non-random attrition.
Norms describe those schools, not the population.
Reference in non-Preleo schools; SES index by school.
Weighting by SES and, for version 1.0, a planned contrast sample.


Criterion built with the same tasks. The persistent difficulty label uses word reading, pseudoword reading and speed.
The validity of those tasks against the label is circular.
Flagged in each task sheet; non-circular criteria (later comprehension, diagnosis recorded in the regional education information system, Séneca).
Alternative label without each task (leave one out at a time).

title: Limitations and data quality
text:
Critique of our own analyses
The analyses in this book also have limitations, and it is better to state them before reviewers do:

Cut-offs have been chosen and evaluated on the same data. Cross-validation across cohorts reduces overfitting, but an external sample is needed.
Stability is not reliability. It mixes measurement error and real change; over one year, it is a lower bound.
The 2021 α values do not document the sample (cohort, session) or the treatment of unreached items.
The structure by age combines different cohorts pair by pair of tasks. It is exploratory; the confirmatory analysis must be done by cohort, with the same children.
The publication texts in the catalog are generated automatically. They serve as drafts, not as final text.

title: Limitations and data quality
text:
Quality classes of each task
So that the manual is honest without discarding valuable data, each task is assigned a quality class with fixed, public rules, computed automatically in the catalog:

Reliability traffic light. Green if α ≥ .80 (only in tasks without a time limit) or stability ρ ≥ .60. Amber if α ≥ .70 or ρ ≥ .40. Red if there are data but they fall short. No data if there is neither α nor stability.
Sample traffic light. Green with at least 500 children in one session and two cohorts; amber with at least 200; red with fewer.
Continuity traffic light. Green with three or more sessions; amber with two; red with one.
Class A: reliability and sample in green, no warnings. Included in the manual with a full task sheet and norms.

title: Limitations and data quality
section: Recommendations for what is measured from now on
text:
Recommendations for what is measured from now on

A measurement plan before each school year: which construct, with which task, how many items, at which time points, with which validity criterion.
Closed, dated versions: any change in items, timing or format creates a new version with its own code.
Always record item by item, with the option chosen and the time of each response, and the start and end of the task.
Automatic checks of keys, times and ranges when each session closes, before computing anything.
Parallel forms and short retest (2–4 weeks) in a subsample, for the reliability of speeded tasks.
Double scoring of a recorded subsample, for inter-rater agreement.
A preregistered analysis plan before confirmatory studies, as has already been done with Preleo.
A single source of truth: the master dictionary and the long table. No hand-copied matrices.

title: Report bands: levels and the watch zone
text:
The five bands
In one sentence. The report for one term places each child in one of five percentile bands. Between P20 and P30 there is no label but monitoring, and the word “difficulty” is reserved for what persists across school years.
The classroom report prototype uses these bands from its version 2 (in Spanish). Compared with version 1, the “mild” band (P17–P25) disappears: what was between P11 and P19 becomes “at risk”, and what was between P20 and P25 becomes “watch”, together with P26–P30.

title: Report bands: levels and the watch zone
text:
Why this way

Fewer label changes due to chance. With a test of reliability .85, the proportion of children whose label changes from one assessment to the next without their having changed drops from 14% to 6% (see The watch zone (in Spanish)).
Each band carries an action. The report does not only classify: it says what to do and when to look again.
It continues the group’s guide. The LEEDUCA early identification guide already proposed graded severity judgments with cut-offs at P10, P20 and P30 for the Grade 1 reading tasks, instead of a single cut-off (Luque 2022).
Bands describe a term; certainty levels describe a trajectory. A child in band 4 for one term does not “have dyslexia”. Persistent difficulty is defined with the whole trajectory from age 6 to 11, with the certainty levels of How we estimate risk. The report for a term speaks of risk and support, not diagnosis.
The error band is visible. Each point in the report carries its margin of error. If a child’s band crosses the limit of their reporting band, the report treats it as the more favorable neighboring band until the next assessment.

title: The Preleo program
text:
What it is
Preleo is a universal prevention program for reading difficulties, designed by the LEEDUCA group at the University of Málaga. It is delivered to the whole class in preschool, before difficulties appear, and not only to children at risk. It starts from a well-established idea: learning to read without difficulty requires a solid foundation in oral language and, above all, in phonological awareness. In Spanish, a language with an almost transparent orthography, syllabic and phonemic awareness are moderately related to word reading, pseudoword reading and comprehension (Míguez-Álvarez, Cuevas-Alonso, and Saavedra 2022).
It has five features:

title: The Preleo program
text:
It is delivered by the teachers themselves in the regular classroom, in daily sessions of 10 to 30 minutes depending on age and activity.
Brief training and ongoing support: teachers receive short initial training and remote follow-up that helps them adapt the activities to their group.
It is sequenced week by week: each school year has a 29-week schedule (October to May) that states which activity from each block corresponds to each week.
It is linked to the LEEDUCA platform: the assessment each term shows how each child is progressing and who needs more support, as in response to intervention (RTI) models.
It fits the curriculum: each block comes with a plan that relates it to the objectives, content, assessment criteria and standards of the Andalusian preschool and primary curriculum.

title: The Preleo program
text:
Materials







Material

Booklet for age 4

For age 3 there is a plan and a schedule (in the platform’s download area), but no booklet of activity sheets among the materials reviewed.

What an activity sheet looks like
All activity sheets follow the same template, designed so that a teacher without specific training can deliver them:

Content, assessment criterion and learning standard, taken from the plan.
Hands on · How do we do it?: aim of the activity and step-by-step procedure, with a script of what the teacher says and a worked example.
Materials: lists of items (words, syllables, sentences, pseudowords) and picture cards, which teachers can replace with others from their own class.
Theoretical rationale for the activity: a short text explaining why it is done (for example, how vocabulary is organized into semantic categories, how gender and verb inflections are acquired in Spanish, or what verbal fluency measures).

Example (age 4, “How many words are there?”): the teacher builds sentences with name cards and action pictograms (“María eats”), the class “reads” them and counts how many words they have. It starts with two-word sentences with proper names and moves on to three words and then to sentences with determiners and prepositions.

title: The Preleo program
text:
Structure
The current version is organized into five blocks worked on in parallel every week.







Block
What is worked on




Phonological awareness
Rhymes; lexical and syntactic awareness (counting the words in a sentence, words within words, compound words); syllabic awareness (identifying the initial, middle and final syllable; counting, blending, deleting, adding, substituting and reversing syllables; stressed syllable); phonemic awareness (counting and segmenting phonemes; blending, deleting and substituting the initial and final phoneme; phoneme synthesis). Manipulations produce both words and pseudowords


Alphabetic principle (age 5)
A sound of the week: identifying whether a word begins or ends with it, discriminating it from similar sounds (phonological contrast) and associating it with its letter. At the end of the year, blending sounds and letters to read words of 3, 4 and 5 phonemes


Vocabulary
Semantic fields and categories, relations between words (part of, generalization, similarities and differences, opposites, function, features), compound words and word families. At age 5, also morphosyntax: gender and number agreement (also with pseudowords), conjugation by person and tense, idioms, and detecting ill-formed sentences


Oral comprehension
Inferences from picture cards (age 4: “The detective game”, “The nosy lion”); at age 5, short oral texts with different types of questions, sentence comprehension depending on word order (“Trick sentences”) and gendered pronouns (“Lola’s game”)


Fluency
Verbal fluency and rapid naming, not reading fluency: quickly naming pictures from a semantic field, or words that begin with the syllable or sound of the week (a traditional Spanish word game), and, at age 5, rapid naming of the letters already learned



Some vocabulary activities also work on cognitive flexibility (switching criteria, for example “profession or means of communication?”).

Progression by age

The weekly sequence
Age 4. After two weeks of syntactic awareness (“How many words are there?”, “Breaking words”, with songs), the year moves through three-week cycles per consonant: P, L, S, M, T, N, D, F and J. In each cycle the initial, final and middle syllable with that consonant are worked on, a song (“The monosyllable”) is sung and children do rapid naming of words beginning with it; the third week closes with the word game. In parallel, each week adds a syllable operation, from easier to harder:

Deleting the first syllable (word and pseudoword); “Dancing syllables”; reversing syllables; adding and deleting the middle syllable



Comprehension: “The detective game” (weeks 1–23) and “The nosy lion” (24–29).
Age 5. Phonological awareness moves from the syllable to the phoneme, and the alphabetic principle advances one sound per week (two for the hardest ones):

From week 22, sounds and letters are blended to read words of 3, 4 and 5 phonemes, and the year ends with “The tree” (word, syllable, phoneme and letter). Comprehension: two oral texts per week (weeks 1–25), one plus “Trick sentences” in weeks 26–27, and “Lola’s game” (28–29). Fluency: rapid naming of words with the sound of the week and, every other week from week 17, of the letters already learned.


Dose
Each school year consists of 29 weeks of daily delivery, with 4 blocks per week at age 4 and 5 at age 5. Neither the booklets nor the plans set the minutes per block: the published reference is 10 to 30 minutes per session (Sánchez-Gómez et al. 2025).

text:
Intervention tiers on the platform
On the platform, Preleo is not only the classroom program. The section “Intervention systems › Preleo” organizes a three-tier response to intervention model, linked by screening each term and weekly monitoring:









Tier
For whom
Format

Tier 1 · Universal
The whole class
Group, in the classroom
Universal program: schedule and plans for ages 3, 4 and 5, with downloadable activity sheets and songs


Tier 2 · Small groups
Children at risk in the screening or with insufficient response
Small group
The content of the universal program, with more intensity and support


Tier 3 · Individualized intervention
Children who do not respond sufficiently to tier 2
Individual, daily
Intensification program, which the specialist individualizes from the system’s suggestions (below)



At all tiers, the review program serves as monitoring. It contains the weeks of the universal program (18 at age 3, 32 at age 4 and 32 at age 5), and each child completes them alone, with their own user account, once a week. It is delivered the week after the one worked on in the group, so that time, accuracy and efficiency serve as a baseline and as a weekly measure of progress.
At CMCI (Barranquilla, Colombia; school year 2026/27), tier 2 is being piloted: three weekly small-group sessions with the current week of the universal program and one individual review session with the following week. Specialists also have access to tier 3 to individualize the intervention.
The platform also includes, with no described use yet, a “LEEDUCA palette” per classroom, and the Leetrea program for learning to read at ages 6 to 8 (universal and review), completed and in the testing phase (see The Leetrea program).

Tier 3 (1): system suggestions, 45 predesigned weeks
Each week is a platform session with five days (Monday to Friday) and a fixed pattern of components repeated every day in the same order. Content and difficulty change. The whole week can be delivered, or only the component flagged by the screening.

The three 15-week blocks follow the same progression as the classroom program for ages 3, 4 and 5. What is specific to intensification is that it works every day on two components that the classroom does not work on systematically: naming speed (RAN) and verbal memory. These are the same domains the screening assesses, and the team’s training material indicates, test by test, in which weeks each weakness is trained (for example, rhymes in week 1, syllable identification in weeks 20 and 26, minimal pairs in weeks 35–45).


Tier 3 (2): individualization by the specialist
The specialist starts from the suggested sequence and adjusts it to the child’s profile: they can deliver only the components flagged by the screening or, for very focused profiles, choose the level of phonological awareness and build their own sequence from the activity index:

Each block has 5 sessions of 5 activities, that is, about 2,100 activities in total.


How decisions are made
According to the team’s training material, moving to a more intensive tier is justified by repeated screening and monitoring, not by a single data point. Support is maintained or withdrawn according to the trajectory, and a child may continue with support after leaving the risk zone if a functional gap with their group remains. The minimum to record is the start date, the reason, the dose and the components. This is exactly what is needed to study the intervention as a dose.
The system’s current suggestions are a fixed sequence that the specialist adapts. Having the system recommend the next session from each child’s data (screening and weekly review) is one of the group’s lines of work.

title: The Preleo program
section: What Preleo trains and what the platform measures
text:
What Preleo trains and what the platform measures
Several Preleo activities practice the same operations assessed by the platform’s phonological awareness tasks at ages 4 and 5 (counting, blending and deleting syllables and phonemes, letter knowledge). A difference on those tasks at the end of preschool is therefore partly near transfer. The demanding test of the program is word reading, pseudoword reading, fluency and comprehension at ages 6 and 7, which the program does not train directly. This is taken into account in the norms (preferred reference: non-Preleo schools) and in the group’s analyses.

title: The Preleo program
text:
Background and published studies
Preleo grew out of the prevention phase of the LEEDUCA Project, implemented in public schools in the province of Málaga since 2013 (Sánchez et al. s. f.). In its first versions, the phonological awareness work relied on MACOFON, a program developed by teachers and speech-language therapists, and was organized into 69 weeks of training. Its theoretical basis is the simple view of reading: decoding and comprehension, supported by phonological awareness and oral language (vocabulary, morphosyntax and comprehension).
It must be understood in context. In a survey of 840 preschool and 876 primary teachers from across Spain, most preferred whole-word methods, attributed phonological awareness to maturity and motivation, and showed limited knowledge of how children learn to read (Giménez et al. 2023). Preleo aims to bring evidence-based instruction to the regular classroom and give teachers a systematic tool.
The group’s studies of its effects:

External evaluation (2014/15 school year). The Andalusian Agency for Educational Evaluation compared 8 LEEDUCA schools with 8 control schools of similar size and socioeconomic index. In Grade 1 it found more children with expressive reading and better comprehension in the LEEDUCA schools (Sánchez et al. s. f.).
Schools of very low socioeconomic status. In two schools with Preleo for 76 weeks (ages 3, 4 and 5) compared with two control schools, with 56 and 63 children, there were improvements in letters at age 5, in the phonological route and then the visual route in Grade 1 (d ≈ 0.44–0.58), and in text speed and intonation in Grade 2 (d ≈ 0.56–0.62). There was no effect on comprehension (Sánchez Gómez, Luque Vilaseca, and Giménez de la Peña 2022).
Regular classrooms (22 schools, ages 4 to 7). Better phonological awareness in the Preleo group and effects on reading one and two years after the program (Sánchez Gómez, Rodríguez Moreno, and Loredo García 2023).
2010 cohort (20 schools, ages 5 to 7). See Sánchez-Gómez et al. (2025).

Using platform data, the group has also studied risk profiles before reading. With phonological awareness, rapid naming, letters and verbal memory at age 5 (795 children), only the profile of globally low performance corresponds to a double deficit, and 92.5% of those children read poorly in Grade 2 (Flores et al. 2026).

title: The Preleo program
text:
Versions delivered
Preleo’s content has changed over the years. This matters when comparing cohorts:

School year 2015/16 (2010 cohort, age 5): only syllabic awareness (10 weeks) and phonemic awareness (19 weeks), from October to May, in the final year of preschool (Sánchez-Gómez et al. 2025). This is a different distribution from the current version at age 5 (4 weeks of syllables and 25 of phonemes).
2011 cohort: from age 4 and over three school years.
Current version: the five blocks described above, from age 3 to 5, with the schedule in the booklets. The fluency and comprehension blocks were added to strengthen the effects on those components of reading.

Pending: edition date of the booklets and the version delivered to each cohort and school; measurement of implementation fidelity.

title: The Leetrea program
text:
What it is
Leetrea is the LEEDUCA group’s program for working on reading at ages 6 to 8 (Grades 1 to 3). It follows on from Preleo, which works on the precursors in preschool, and, like Preleo, it is hosted on the LEEDUCA platform, alongside the assessment tasks.

Screening. The platform’s tasks for ages 6 to 11 are part of the Leetrea screening. The reading, speed and comprehension task sheets in this manual are therefore also the technical basis of the program.
Tiers. On the platform, Leetrea has a universal part (for the whole class) and a review part (for the children who need it), like Preleo.

title: Task catalog
text:
How it is generated
This catalog brings together in one place the 126 platform tasks of the 2010–2015 cohorts (110 assessment tasks; the rest are experimental or under review). For each task it states what it measures, how it is administered, the codes it has in the data, the sessions and ages in which it was given, the measures it records and its psychometric properties. Each one includes a paragraph ready for the instruments section of an article, in Spanish and in English.
How to use it. Search by name, code or construct, or filter by domain or by task family (the measurement model the tasks share; in Spanish). Click on a task to see its summary sheet. The “Copy” buttons copy the paragraph to the clipboard. The full table can be downloaded: Catalogo.csv (one row per task) and Sesiones.csv (one row per task, cohort and session).
What each field means.
The catalog is built with scripts/R/catalogo_tareas.R from four sources:
Stability is recomputed from the long table of scores. No items or answer keys are published: only a general description of the instructions.

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
In brief
Risk should not be a single overall score, but two: risk of dyslexia and risk of developmental language disorder (DLD), each with its own tests. All children take a brief screening; those who are flagged complete the battery, and that is when the profile (dyslexia, oral language or both) and the response are decided.
crumbs: 22  Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
Why two risks

Reading comprehension has two components, word recognition and oral language comprehension (Hoover and Gough 1990). The precursors of the first (letters, phonological awareness, RAN) are not those of the second (vocabulary and grammar) (Storch and Whitehurst 2002; Hulme et al. 2015).
DLD is common and often goes unnoticed. In population studies it affects about 7% of children at school entry (Tomblin et al. 1997; Norbury et al. 2016), and it is associated with more reading difficulties, especially in comprehension.
Dyslexia and DLD overlap, but they are not the same: a child may decode well and understand poorly, or the reverse. Separating the two risks guides intervention better.
crumbs: 22  Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
The two-stage circuit





flowchart LR
  A["All students<br/>key tests"] --> B{"Below<br/>the cut-off?"}
  B -- no --> C["Regular instruction<br/>(Tier 1)"]
  B -- yes --> D["Full battery<br/>in the same session"]
  D --> E["Dyslexia profile<br/>Tier 2 reading"]
  D --> F["Oral language profile<br/>language support"]
  D --> G["Both<br/>reading and language"]







Universal screening. The key dyslexia tests (letter knowledge, phonological awareness and RAN), plus two brief oral language tasks in all schools: one for vocabulary and one for grammar. Better a few well-measured tasks than many poorly measured ones.
Second stage. Those below the cut-off for either risk complete the battery, including oral language, in the same session whenever possible. This is the two-stage screening model (Compton et al. 2010).
Profile and response. The profile is assigned with the full battery, not with the screening.
crumbs: 22  Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
Oral language tasks for screening








Component
Task
Why




Vocabulary
Vocabulary: definitions (1705)
It is the platform’s oral language task with the most items and the highest reliability


Grammar
Grammatical reception (1542)
It covers morphosyntax, the second domain required by DLD criteria. It has 21 items (plus one practice item), is administered from age 4 and is on the current platform, so it can be repeated in every school year



Together they cover the two aspects required by CATALISE: expressive vocabulary and receptive grammar (Bishop et al. 2017). Sentence ordering (193) remains an alternative grammar task from age 6; it has only 5 items and a ceiling.
The same tasks in every school year. Monitoring only compares like with like if the tasks do not change from one school year to the next. While the old versions are being replaced, scores are expressed in a common indicator (proportion correct or correct per minute) and as a percentile within each age and term.
The sentence comprehension and multiple-choice vocabulary tasks are not recommended for decisions about an individual child, because of their low reliability. The morphology tasks have a ceiling effect at age 5.
crumbs: 22  Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
Oral language levels
The levels follow the same logic as those for reading difficulty (How we estimate risk): a low score in a single assessment is not enough; it must be repeated. The cut-offs are taken from the large population studies of DLD: −1.25 SD in EpiSLI (Tomblin, Records, and Zhang 1996) and −1.5 SD in SCALES (Norbury et al. 2016). Persistence is what the CATALISE consensus requires (Bishop et al. 2017).








Level
Rule
Response




TL-A
Vocabulary or grammar below −1.5 SD (≈ P7) in at least two school years
Referral for speech-language assessment


TL-B
Oral language ≤ P25 in at least two school years
Classroom language support (Tier 2) and monitoring


TR
Oral language ≤ P25 in some school year
Monitoring at the next assessment


INT / TE
Never ≤ P25
Regular instruction
crumbs: 22  Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language

title: Screening for two risks: dyslexia and oral language
text:
Caveats

A platform level is not a diagnosis of DLD. Diagnosis requires a speech-language assessment and information on development, context and functional impact (Bishop et al. 2017).
No labeling based on a single assessment. Oral language changes a great deal between ages 4 and 6, and the platform’s tasks have few items.
When oral language is low, reading should also be monitored, because the two risks often go together.
Cut-offs and tasks may change once the validation results with the platform data are published.

title: Reading speed in words per minute
text:
0. Theoretical framework: from speed to comprehension
Words correct per minute (WCPM) is a unit that teachers and families understand, and it can be computed for all reading tasks on the platform. In the 2010–2015 cohorts, the median of the non-Preleo group for text read aloud goes from 50 WCPM at the end of Grade 1 to about 100 WCPM at the end of Grade 2. With isolated words, from 36 to 69 WCPM between the end of Grade 1 and the end of Grade 3.
Three caveats before using it:
This is a draft to test the task sheet structure with widely used tasks. Script: scripts/velocidad_lectora.py; output: velocidad_lectora_v1.xlsx.
What fluency is. Reading fluently means reading accurately, at a good pace and with the intonation that the meaning of the text requires. Speed is only one of its parts. In the simple view of reading, fluency is the bridge between decoding and comprehension: if recognizing words takes little effort, resources are left for understanding (Hoover and Gough 1990).
What the evidence in Spanish says:
Why the two EDICOLE readings matter. Children adjust the way they read to the goal. Faced with a meaningful text they adopt a fluent reading that is hard to modify; with isolated words, on the other hand, they follow instructions to go slower or faster more readily (Bowey 1984). Reading silently speeds up text processing. This harms comprehension if the child regulates their own reading, but the effect disappears if it is ensured that the child processes the text (Carretti et al. 2012). In addition, comprehension measured as correct responses per minute is more closely related to word reading than comprehension measured as correct responses alone (Rønberg and Petersen 2016).
What it implies for the platform:
crumbs: 24  Reading speed in words per minute

title: Reading speed in words per minute
text:
Fluency is one of the components most closely related to comprehension. In a meta-analysis of 33 studies with monolingual Spanish-speaking children, the strongest relations with comprehension were those of fluency and phonological awareness (Baker et al. 2022).
The weight of speed decreases across school years. In Spanish children, automaticity in word reading explains comprehension mainly in Grade 2; in Grade 4 prosody gains weight (Calet, Gutiérrez-Palma, and Defior 2015). In Chilean children in Grades 2 and 3, vocabulary and oral comprehension weighed more than speed (Quezada et al. 2024). This is the pattern of the simple view in a transparent orthography: decoding is mastered early and language takes over afterwards (Sánchez-Vincitore et al. 2022; Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018).
Prosody keeps its relation with comprehension. A meta-analysis in Spanish speakers estimates it at r = .46, the same in primary and secondary school (Roldán et al. 2022). In Grade 4, text prosody, and not speed, added to the explanation of comprehension beyond decoding and language (Veenendaal, Groen, and Verhoeven 2015).
Fluency can be improved. In Spanish speakers from the final year of preschool to Grade 6, interventions on speed or fluency have a mean effect of 0.47 (Ripoll Salceda and Zevallos Polo 2024).




The weak relation between EDICOLE speed and comprehension (ρ = .1–.3) is not a flaw of the task. It is what is expected when decoding is already mastered and the text is short.
The second reading makes it possible to measure comprehension as efficiency (correct responses per minute of reading) and to check whether the child adjusts their pace to the goal. This is the idea of experiment E8 in § 4 sexies.
The platform does not measure prosody, which is the component that remains most closely tied to comprehension. Recording the text reading (at least in a subsample) would make it possible to score it.

Update of October 19 (J. L. Luque): the two EDICOLE readings have different instructions. In the first, children are asked to read quickly (“text read aloud”). In the second, they are asked to read slowly to answer questions (“reading for comprehension”). It is the same text: it has the same number of words and lines in both measures, in both form A and form B. This changes how reading for comprehension is interpreted:

It is a rereading. It comes out 15–30 WCPM faster even though children are asked to go slowly. Most likely familiarity with the text (a rereading effect) plays a role, and perhaps also silent reading.
It is not comparable with the silent reading of published norms, which is always a first reading (§ 4 bis).
The difference between the two readings is an implicit experiment. It measures the gain from rereading and whether the child adjusts their speed to the task (E8, § 4 sexies).

It remains to be confirmed whether the second reading is silent and whether the child sees the questions before reading.

3. Reliability
Forms A and B at the same time point. This is a classic use of Bland-Altman: two versions of the same test, given to the same child on the same day.






Figure 24.2: EDICOLE forms A and B (Bland-Altman; labels in Spanish).




On the old platform (6.3 and 7.3) the forms are reliable (r = .86–.90), but not equivalent: form B yields 5–14 WCPM more. There are two possible explanations: form B is easier, or the line-based count is not the same (9 long lines vs. 11 short ones). For the norms, each form needs its own table or an equating equation.
On the new platform (8.2–11.2) agreement collapses (r = .40–.51) and the limits of agreement widen from ±30 to ±100 WCPM. Test–retest between 7.2 and 8.2 in 2011 is r = .27, with a mean drop of 50 WCPM, which is impossible. What the time counts in those versions (10737, 10740, 10738 and 10741) needs to be checked with the platform engineer: whether it includes the instructions, whether it is timed differently, or whether the key is pressed differently. What it shows:

Reading aloud, Grades 1, 2 and 4 match the meta-analysis. In Grade 3 we are about 20 WCPM faster. There are three explanations, not mutually exclusive: the Grade 3 figure comes from a single cohort (2010, N = 140); our text is short (62–68 words) and simple; and our WCPM counts correct lines, not correct words, and Ripoll finds that measures in words per minute give higher values than those in words correct in Grades 1–3.
Reading for comprehension is 15–25 WCPM faster than the silent reading in the meta-analysis, but the comparison is not valid. According to J. L. Luque, it is the second reading of the same text (§ 1), whereas the meta-analysis covers first readings. Moreover, there are only 2–4 studies per grade there, and in our data the time ends when the child presses the key. For comparison with the literature, text read aloud (first reading) is used.
PROLEC-R fits our lists. In Grade 2, its “slow” category in word reading is equivalent to 26–33 WCPM; in our norms for 7.2, P10 is 25 and P25 is 37. For pseudowords, its Grade 2 “slow” is equivalent to 18–22 WCPM, between our P10 (16) and P25 (24). They are different tasks (40 words of varying length vs. 12 two-syllable words), but PROLEC-R “slowness” falls roughly at our P10–P20.
The original EDICOLE is a silent reading test administered in groups, according to the material in the test folder. On the platform, the same text is read twice with different instructions (quickly, and slowly to answer questions). It remains to be confirmed with the engineer whether the second reading is silent.

The most relevant point for publication: Ripoll et al. (2020) point to the scarcity of speed data referring to a specific term as a major gap, and they find differences between terms in Grades 1 and 2. LEEDUCA has three measurements per school year, with Ns in the hundreds per time point. WCPM norms by term from Grade 1 to Grade 3 fill exactly that gap.

title: Reading speed in words per minute
section: 4 ter. Does speed have a ceiling?
text:
4 ter. Does speed have a ceiling?
There are two different questions.
First: does speed level off with age? Yes. An exponential curve with an asymptote fitted to the means of the meta-analysis (Grade 1 to Year 11) gives a ceiling of about 200 WCPM reading aloud (95% CI: 163–236) and about 211 WCPM reading silently (190–231). Brysbaert (2019) places adults at 183 WCPM reading aloud and 238 silently. Reading aloud, the limit is set largely by speech rate; reading silently, the curve keeps rising into adolescence. Our medians for Grades 1 to 3 fall on the steep part of the curve. Estimating the ceiling with our own data would require the time points at ages 9–11, which are not reliable today (new platform).






Figure 24.4: Curve with a ceiling, and gain of the same children between terms (labels in Spanish).



With the same children measured twice, the mean gain in text read aloud is 12 WCPM per term. From May to November there are 6 months, with the summer in between and about two and a half months of school, and the gain is almost the same (13 WCPM). Summer does not make children lose speed, but it does not make it grow either. Note: comparing medians of different time points gave a misleading “flat summer”, because it mixed cohorts and dropouts. That is why the gain is always computed with paired data.
Second: does the child perform better if hurried? That is another question. With more time pressure, speed is usually gained and accuracy lost. In slow readers in Grades 2 and 4, rising from about 35 to about 90 WCPM was not accompanied by better comprehension (O’Connor, 2018, cited in Ripoll et al., 2020). All we have is a weak natural experiment: letter task 535 had a 60 s limit on the old platform and none on the new one, and efficiency at the same age is similar. These are different cohorts, so it is not proof. If of interest, the platform would allow a clean experiment: the same text with and without a visible timer, randomly assigned within each classroom.

The sentence for teachers and families comes from the multiplier: what takes an adult 10 minutes of reading takes a Grade 2 child at the 10th percentile about 43, and a typical child about 25. It is a figure computed from our own data. What is missing is how many words a child reads per day in class. It can be measured by counting the words in a week’s materials in two or three classrooms: a simple, new data point of our own.
The limits of this estimate: speed is measured with short, easy texts; with long texts fatigue appears, and comprehension adds time. It must be presented as an estimate, not as a diagnosis.
Can a child’s progress be seen within one term? Hardly ever. In text read aloud, the typical child gains 12 WCPM per term, but a change of about 29 WCPM is needed to distinguish it from measurement error at 90%. For isolated words: 7 vs. 16. This is the figure that calls for the most humility in a report. Individual progress is seen over a school year, not a term. Three decisions for the report follow from this:

report the trend with three or more measurements, not the difference between two;
flag as change only what departs from the expected gain by more than the threshold;
study whether averaging forms A and B raises reliability enough to shorten the interval.

Reliability
See § 3: test–retest between terms with Bland-Altman and the reliable change threshold, and EDICOLE forms A and B. Internal consistency is missing: the lists have item-level responses and times on the new platform (_res, _di), so α and ω can be computed (E5).


Predictive validity without circularity
The problem. The reading difficulty label (DL-A/B, school years at ages 6–11) is built from words, pseudowords and text speed. If a measure at ages 6 to 8 “predicts” that label, it partly predicts itself: AUCs come out between 0.85 and 0.95 (sheet 3_Validez_predictiva, rows 3c) and must not be presented as predictive validity. Two criteria that do not contain the measure are used:

3a. Measure at age 5 against the label at ages 6–11. It is the same kind of task, but measured earlier and with data that do not enter the label.
3b. Measure at age 6 against poor comprehension (≤ P25 of the non-Preleo group) at least one school year later. Comprehension is not part of the label.

How to read it:

At age 5, speed on the lists predicts later reading difficulty very well (AUC 0.80–0.85). A simple cut-off that a teacher can understand (“reads no word in the 3rd term of the final year of preschool”) identifies 3 out of 4 children with difficulty, with 18% false positives.
Speed at age 6 predicts later comprehension poorly (AUC 0.56–0.64). This is to be expected: comprehension also depends on oral language (simple view of reading). In addition, the comprehension criterion is a score based on few questions and of low reliability, which lowers the AUC. It is a lower bound.
For reviewers: the AUC against the label from age 6 is presented only as agreement with the criterion, never as prediction.

SES weighs more on speed than on letters or RAN (d ≈ 0.35–0.45 vs. ≈ 0.2). It is significant at almost all time points. This makes sense: fluency depends on how much one reads, and that varies with the environment.

Preleo does not change speed consistently at any time point.
Sex: a result to be checked. Girls come out somewhat slower on the lists (d ≈ −0.10; p < .05 at 7 of 20 time points). This runs against what is usual in Spanish, where girls equal or outperform boys. Before interpreting it, the coding of sex in the master list (H/M) must be checked again against Base_4_anios (V/H/M), where H means different things (data issue).

Continuous norms and floor effect (study M3, November 3, 2026)



For text reading speed (form 2034), continuous norms by age deviate systematically within the school year. With cNORM by age, 22% of children fall below P10 at 6.3 and only 4% at 7.3. Using months of instruction, the same method stays between 8% and 13% at all time points. The table by time point remains the published reference; the continuous model on months of instruction is proposed for intermediate dates. Floor: 8% zeros at 6.3.

5. Use in the classroom and in the report; pending tasks
In the server report, the result can be given like this: “Reads 45 words per minute aloud; half of their school year reads 77 or more (15th percentile)”. The “minutes for 1,000 words” column makes it possible to estimate how long each student will take to read a text. For example, a 300-word text takes a typical Grade 2 child about 4 minutes, and more than twice as long for a child at P10.

title: Letter knowledge
text:
1. Task description
Pilot task: letter knowledge (LEC_LETRAS). It is the most widely administered of the predictors: 10,241 valid administrations in 5 cohorts (2010–2014) and 8 time points (4.2–6.1). It is also the task with the most weight in the age-5 model of article L2 (OR 0.37 per SD). The task sheet computes all indicators with a reproducible script, scripts/ficha_piloto_letras.py, which produces ficha_LET_v1.xlsx.
Results in one line:
Two data issues must be corrected before publication (section 7).
The child names letters that appear on the screen one at a time, in random order. Either the letter name or its sound is accepted. The examiner marks a correct response with the left mouse button and an error with the right one. If the child takes more than 5 s on a letter, it counts as an error. Process: phonological route, alphabetic knowledge (Reading domain).
Main measure: efficiency, in correct letters per minute (efi on the old platform, ve on the new one). Correct responses, errors and time are also recorded.
Instruction to the child (67): “Now you are going to see some letters. I know you are very fast, so tell me as fast as you can which letter appears on the screen.”
Not part of the task, although the dictionary groups them under LEC_LETRAS:

title: Letter knowledge
section: 1 bis. Theoretical framework: what letter knowledge measures and why it matters
text:
1 bis. Theoretical framework: what letter knowledge measures and why it matters
Letter knowledge is the ability to recognize each grapheme and say its name or sound. It is the child’s first contact with the alphabetic principle, the idea that letters represent speech sounds. Without that connection there can be no decoding. Together with phonological awareness and rapid naming (RAN), it is one of the three major predictors of reading and of dyslexia in alphabetic languages. All three keep their predictive value in languages with very different orthographies (Ozernov-Palchik et al., 2017; Caravolas et al., 2012).
The longitudinal evidence is consistent on four points:

It is the best predictor before formal instruction. In family-risk studies, letter knowledge at age 4 was the best predictor of reading level at age 6 (Gallagher, Frith & Snowling, 2000). At age 5 it was the variable that best anticipated who would develop reading difficulty (Pennington & Lefly, 2001).
What it predicts is the learning trajectory. The Jyväskylä study distinguished “delayed”, “linear” and “early” letter-learning trajectories between ages 4.5 and 6.5. The delayed trajectory predicted poor reading in Grade 1 and was more frequent in children at family risk (Torppa et al., 2006). This supports measuring letters several times per school year, as LEEDUCA does, rather than once.
It works the same way in Spanish. Knowledge of letter–sound correspondences predicts reading with similar weight in English, Spanish, Czech and Slovak (Caravolas et al., 2012, 2013). In Spanish, fluency in letter naming was the best precursor of early reading (De la Calle et al., 2021).
It depends on the environment. It is predicted by explicit letter instruction and the family’s educational level, and socioeconomic status modifies which precursors weigh most (Torppa et al., 2006; Escobar & Meneses, 2014). That is why the result should be interpreted with reference to the school SES index and exact age.

A measurement caveat: it is a “constrained” skill, with few items that almost all children master by the time they reach primary school. It therefore discriminates a lot in preschool and loses discrimination as it reaches ceiling (Bowles, Skibbe & Justice, 2011).
What the LEEDUCA data show (about 10,000 administrations in 5 cohorts):

Prediction. Letters at age 5 predict persistent reading difficulty with an AUC of .80–.82. They are the predictor with the most weight in the age-5 model (OR 0.37 per SD), ahead of phonological awareness. RAN adds no prediction once letters are included.
Ceiling. The uppercase form reaches ceiling at age 5; the 52-letter form does not.
Age and SES. The result depends on relative age (children born in the first half of the year score d ≈ 0.2–0.3 higher at ages 4–5) and on the school SES index. It does not depend on Preleo or on sex.

The pattern matches the international and Spanish literature. It justifies including the task in universal screening from age 4, with norms adjusted for age and SES.
References: Bowles, Skibbe & Justice (2011), J. Appl. Meas.; Caravolas et al. (2012), Psychol. Sci., doi:10.1177/0956797611434536; Caravolas et al. (2013), Psychol. Preleo and SES are confounded in 2013. In the 2013 mixed model (2,571 administrations, 570 children, 22 schools), Preleo appears to subtract when unadjusted (b = −0.36 SD).
