section: 6 ter. How to store the norms for the server
text:
6 ter. How to store the norms for the server
Proposed common format for all tasks, with letters as the first example (04_DICCIONARIO_PROCESADO_2026/BAREMOS_SERVIDOR/, script exportar_baremos.py):

Cut-off table (baremos_LEC_LETRAS_v1.csv), for phase 1 with fixed norms. It has one row per task × code × measure × school year × term × stratum × percentile (1–99), with the minimum raw score for each percentile. Strata are “general” (non-Preleo reference) and “low / medium / high SES” when there are at least 100 children. It is a single table for all tasks: the server imports it directly and computes the percentile with a query.
Difficulty levels (niveles_dificultad_v1.csv): no difficulty (> P25), mild (P17–25), moderate (P11–16), severe (P6–10) and very severe (≤ P5).
Continuous model (baremos_LEC_LETRAS_modelo_v1.json), for phase 2 with dynamic norms. It stores the coefficients of the quantile regression of the score on age in months and SES for percentiles 1–99. This way the server can give the percentile at any age and SES and refit the coefficients with new data.

The table and the model agree on the P16 cut-off in 83–95% of cases. The publication version of the model will be built with cNORM (R).
The document ESQUEMA_BAREMOS_v1.md describes the columns, use, update rules and the questions for the engineer:

How does the server store norms today?
Does it know the pupil’s date of birth and school?
Can it run R or Python?

title: Letter knowledge
section: 6 quater. Rigor: agreement between terms, reliable change, precision of the percentile and differential prediction
text:
6 quater. Rigor: agreement between terms, reliable change, precision of the percentile and differential prediction
Everything comes from scripts/rigor_tarea.py (reusable functions for any task), with output in rigor_LET_v1.xlsx and figures F2–F4. There are two new conclusions that change decisions:

A single term of letters is not enough to claim that a child has improved or worsened.
The SES-adjusted percentile should not be used to decide risk.

Agreement between terms (Bland-Altman).






Figure 25.2: Agreement between terms (Bland-Altman; labels in Spanish).




The mean difference between terms is the group’s learning: between +1 and +8 letters/min over 3–6 months. It is smallest between 4.2 and 4.3 and largest at the start of age 5.
The limits of agreement are wide: a child can vary between −10 and +25 letters/min from one term to the next without the task failing.
There is proportional bias at the start of learning (2013 5.1→5.2 and 2014 4.3→5.1): those who already know more letters gain more, a “Matthew effect”. It disappears from 5.2.

Reliable change (RCI, 90%).






Figure 25.3: Reliable change index (labels in Spanish).




To claim that a child has really changed, a change of 11–15 letters/min above the group’s mean gain is needed; 7 in the best case.
That is why only 3–10% of children change reliably between two terms.
For the server: the monitoring report should not flag “improves” or “worsens” with two data points from this task alone. The RCI, the trend over 3 or more time points or a composite of tasks must be used.

Precision of the percentile. The standard error of measurement is 4.6–6.0 letters/min. With a 90% CI:

a child at P16 at ages 4–5 is in fact between P0 and P35–49;
at 6.1, between P3 and P30;
in the middle of the distribution, a P50 ranges from P27 to P74 (sheet 2_IC_percentiles).

This reinforces two decisions: report the percentile with its band, and do not classify on the basis of a single task but of the composite (phonological awareness + letters + RAN), as in the L2 model.
Differential prediction (Cleary).






Figure 25.4: Differential prediction by sex and SES (labels in Spanish).




Sex: the task predicts equally well for boys and girls. Neither the intercept (p = .32) nor the slope (p = .17) differ; AUC .84 and .79. No norms by sex are needed.
SES: the slope is the same (p = .15), but the intercept is not (p = .002). With the same letter score, a child from a low-SES school has a higher risk of persistent reading difficulty (prevalence 20.5% vs. 11.3% in high SES).
Therefore, separate SES-based norms would place those children higher and hide real risk precisely where there is most. The right approach is to keep the risk cut-off with the general non-Preleo norms. The SES-based percentile, if given, is context only.
A caveat for the team: the difficulty label is not adjusted for SES either. The higher risk in low SES may reflect both real disadvantage and a stricter criterion for those children. It should be checked with an external criterion (clinical diagnosis) when we have one.

Pending: differential item functioning (DIF) of each letter by sex and SES, once item-level responses are available.






Continuous norms and floor effect (study M3, November 3, 2026)



The continuous model in this task sheet (quantile regression on age in months) was compared with five other methods. For letters, the axis matters little: within each time point, the error in P10 is 1.6–2.1 points with any continuous method, compared with 0.5 for the table by time point. Out of sample, the best method is cNORM on months of instruction (mean error 3.3 points, compared with 4.0 for the model by age), and it covers all children, whereas the table only covers 76%. It is proposed to move the server model to the instruction axis for consistency with the reading tasks, where age does distort calibration. The floor for letters does not exceed 6% (at 4.2).
Details in study M3.

title: Letter knowledge
section: 7. Pending issues and decisions for the team
text:
7. Pending issues and decisions for the team
Data issues found while building the task sheet (added to the Issues sheet of the dictionary):

Code 1887 is averaged with letters in certeza_cortes_baremos_v2. Code 1887 is the note “how does the child read the letters?”. Because of this error, the LET score of 2010 and 2011 (6.1) and of 2013 (4.3 and 5.2) is halved. The rank order of the children barely changes (ρ = .92–.98), so the effect on L2 should be small. Even so, v3 must be generated without 1887 and L2 rerun before submission.
Code 5431 (RAN letters card, 2014) is labeled LEC_LETRAS. It must move to RAN.
Form 535 is not administered the same way on the two platforms. On the old one (2010–2011) it stops at 60 s; on the new one (2012–2014) it presents all 28 letters with no limit (up to 300 s). Efficiency is comparable, but correct responses are not.
The instruction for 535 says it “is only given if the child can read uppercase letters”. It must be confirmed whether a 0 at age 4 means “does not know letters” or “not administered”. This affects the floor and P5.

Missing data:

School SES for all cohorts. Resolved on October 17 with the 2010, 2011 and 2013 matrices (section 6 bis): 93–100% coverage in 2010–2013.
SES for 2014–2015: only about 50% coverage, because school names are written differently (e.g., “CEIP Al- Ándalus” vs. “Al-Andalus (Marbella)”). These names still need to be unified; San Ceferino has no SES.
Sex coding checked on October 17: in the master list H = boy and M = girl; in Base_4_anios V = boy and H/M = girl.
Review the dates of birth of the 2012 cohort: resolved on October 19 (it was a format reading error).
Item-level responses (Respuestas_usuario) to compute α/ω and the difficulty of each letter.

To decide with Juan Luis:

Can this task sheet serve as a template for the other tasks? It contains description, sample, descriptives, reliability, validity, non-Preleo norms and an analysis of whether the norms should be adjusted.
How should SES be adjusted for? There are two options: continuous norms with SES as a covariate (cNORM) or a complementary percentile by SES band.

title: TECLE
text:
Description
In one sentence. TECLE measures reading efficiency: it is stable from one school year to the next, it distinguishes children with diagnosed dyslexia very well (AUC = .86), and its items work the same on paper and on the platform (r = .99). But it anticipates comprehension poorly, and the platform version has five items with the correct answer wrongly recorded.
Each item shows a sentence with its last word missing. The child reads silently and chooses, from four words, the one that completes the sentence. There are 64 sentences of increasing difficulty and 5 minutes: almost nobody finishes, so the score mainly reflects how many sentences the child reads correctly in that time.
On the platform, correct responses per minute are used because the actual time varies by a few seconds between children (272–302 s). With 5 minutes, 1 correct response per minute is equivalent to about 5 correct responses.

title: TECLE
text:
Theoretical framework and evidence
TECLE is a brief, group-administered test of reading efficiency: within a fixed time, the child reads sentences silently and completes each one by choosing a word. To get it right, the child has to decode quickly and understand just enough to pick the word that fits. It is the same type of task as English-language silent sentence reading tests such as the TOSREC.
What the evidence says:

Origin. M. S. Carrillo and J. Marín designed TECLE in 1997, with the collaboration of J. Alegría and A. R. Calvo, as a research instrument. It is inspired by Lobrot’s L3 test, but it is not an adaptation: it has 24 more sentences, mostly short ones, so that it discriminates from the first school years. In addition, in each item two distractors are pseudowords and one is a word, all very similar to the correct word. This makes the test depend heavily on decoding and makes it useful for detecting difficulties, including dyslexia.
As the first stage of screening. In Molina de Segura (Murcia), TECLE was administered in groups to 1,894 schoolchildren in Grades 2, 4 and 6 as the first stage of dyslexia screening. The cut-off at mean − 1.5 SD was equivalent to about two years of reading delay. 96% of the children it flagged then showed a phonological or orthographic deficit in the individual assessment (Carrillo Gallego et al. 2011). This is the most direct evidence of its validity for screening in Spanish.
The group’s norms. The paper normative study was carried out with 6,492 schoolchildren in Grades 2 to 6 from 53 schools in Málaga, assessed in November (Carrillo et al. 2024). These are the same paper data as in this task sheet, and that manual is the reference for interpreting paper scores.
Duration. In Spain it is administered in 5 minutes. With older students, and in other studies, 3 minutes have been used; those scores are not comparable with 5-minute scores.
Adaptations in other Spanish-speaking countries. There is a Uruguayan technical manual (Cuadro et al., 2009) and an Argentine adaptation with 693 students in Grades 5 to 7. In the latter, item difficulty was adequate and the score depended on grade and educational opportunities, but not on sex (Ferreres et al., 2011).
Silent sentence reading tests are useful for screening. The validity of the TOSREC as a screener in response-to-intervention models has been studied specifically (Johnson et al., 2011). In secondary school, a group sentence verification test classified almost as well as individual oral fluency (Denton et al., 2011).
In the first school years it mainly measures decoding. In Grade 1, silent and oral fluency are related but distinct skills (Kim, Wagner & Foster, 2011). In poor readers in Grade 4, decoding and fluency explain only 22% of the TOSREC (Kang & Shin, 2019).

What our data say agrees: at ages 7–8, TECLE is closely related to word and text reading and weakly to comprehension; it depends somewhat on school socioeconomic status and hardly on sex, as in the Argentine adaptation.
What TECLE measures within the simple view of reading. It is a timed sentence comprehension task, so its score is an efficiency: sentences understood per unit of time. When comprehension is measured as a rate, and not only as correct responses, it depends more on word recognition (Rønberg and Petersen 2016). That is why in the first school years TECLE behaves mainly as a decoding measure, and its relation with language should increase with age, as the simple view predicts (Hoover and Gough 1990; Sánchez-Vincitore et al. 2022). In our paper data, the relation with the Spanish language grade drops from .53 in Grade 2 to .36 in Grade 6. This fits with text comprehension in the higher grades depending increasingly on language, something a test of simple sentences does not capture. TECLE is useful for screening reading efficiency throughout primary school, but it does not replace a measure of text comprehension.
References located with SciSpace (volumes and pages still to be checked): Cuadro et al. (2009), Ciencias Psicológicas; Denton et al. (2011), Scientific Studies of Reading; Ferreres et al. (2011), Revista Neuropsicología Latinoamericana; Johnson et al. (2011), Assessment for Effective Intervention; Kang & Shin (2019), Reading & Writing Quarterly; Kim, Wagner & Foster (2011), Scientific Studies of Reading.

With all grades together, the AUC is .86 and the difference is 1.3 SD. Almost 6 in 10 children with dyslexia and 1 in 10 of the rest fall below the 10th percentile of their grade. A Grade 6 child with dyslexia reads, on average, like a Grade 4 child. This is known-groups validity, with two caveats: the groups with dyslexia are small, and the Séneca diagnosis depends on the school having requested it.


The same items on paper and on the platform



Difficulty of each item on paper (Grade 2) and on the platform (age 7) (labels in Spanish).



The 22 sentences that enough children reach in both formats have the same difficulty on paper and on the platform (r = .99). On the platform they are somewhat harder (4 percentage points fewer correct), a small difference that may be due to format or cohort (both groups are in Grade 2).
Data issue: the platform’s answer key. For items 15 and 19, on paper 86–88% of those who reach them get them right, and on the platform 5–6%. The platform also stores which option each child chose, which makes it possible to check: for items 15, 19, 36 and 37, 81–90% of children choose the booklet’s correct option, but the platform accepts a different one. The same happens with item 51, although only 9 children reach it. These are errors in the recorded key, not in the children.
Item 31, to be checked. The key matches the paper one, but 77% of children choose another option, and on paper almost all get it right. Most likely the options appear on screen in a different order than in the booklet.
What it implies: with the paper key, 7-year-olds go from 17.4 to 18.8 correct on average. The score of 8 in 10 children changes, but the rank order barely does (r = .995), and only 2.2% cross the 25th percentile. The effect is on the level: the platform norms are somewhat lower than they should be.



The platform on the paper scale
The platform records correct responses, errors and time, so its score can be expressed in the same way as on paper: correct − errors/3. This lets readers compare directly with the normative manual. No adjustment for time is needed: the test always lasts 5 minutes, and the time the platform stores is that of the last response.

It measures the same thing as correct responses per minute. The correlation between the two scores is .94–.99 in all sessions. Moving to the paper scale does not change the rank order of the children; it only makes comparison easier.
Levels are similar. Differences from paper for the same grade range from d = -0.38 to 0.30, and between 20% and 39% of platform children fall below the paper P25 (25% if they were equal).
But the causes cannot be separated. Format, cohort and time point go together: the paper data are from November 2020, after the lockdown, and the platform data from 2017–2020. In addition, the new-platform sessions have not yet been rescored with the correct key, which adds a little more than one correct response on average.
Proposal: give both scores in the task sheet, correct responses per minute and correct − errors/3, and build the platform norms on the paper scale once all sessions have been rescored.



Reliability: a speeded test



Difficulty of each item (proportion correct among those who reach it), by grade and format (labels in Spanish).


Almost all sentences are easy for whoever reaches them: the hard part is reaching them. That is why, in a speeded test, internal consistency is misleading:

with all 64 items, α = .91–.95, and the odd–even split gives more than .95. These are inflated: a child who does not reach an item scores zero on it and on all the following ones;
with only the items reached by 90% of the grade, α = .64–.77 and ω = .63–.78. These are deflated: they are very easy items with almost no variance.

The normative manual warns of the same thing and estimates reliability by test–retest: r = .87–.91 with a four-week interval and .64–.80 with one year (Carrillo et al. 2024). In our data, stability between administrations is similar: r = .67–.70 from age 7 to 8 on the platform, and r = .57 between the platform in November 2019 and paper in November 2020 in the same 107 children (with a year, a change of format and the lockdown in between).

Distribution. At age 7, median of 16 correct (3.2 per minute) and about 7 errors. At age 8, 21 correct (4.3 per minute). No floor or ceiling.
Concurrent validity. It is related mainly to words, pseudowords and text speed (r = .69 at age 7 and .79 at age 8). Less to phonological awareness (.38–.45) and little to reading comprehension (.17–.29).
Against the persistent difficulty label, the AUC is .90–.92. But the label is built with TECLE, so this is agreement, not predictive validity.

That is precisely why it is the task that most needs continuous norms to cover the intermediate grades: they will be built when the 2014–2015 cohorts and the 2020–2026 server data are added.

Scientific: a widely used test in Spanish, with items that work the same in two formats.

title: Initial letter identification
text:
Theoretical framework
Letter knowledge is the ability to recognize each grapheme and associate it with its name or sound. It is the gateway to the alphabetic principle. The platform measures it in two ways: naming letters, and choosing the letter with which the name of a picture begins, which also requires isolating the first sound.
What the evidence says. Together with phonological awareness and rapid naming, it is one of the three major predictors of reading. Its weight is similar in English, Spanish and Czech (Caravolas et al. 2013). In Spanish, letter knowledge is the best predictor of simple syllable reading; phonological awareness weighs more for complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020). The full review of the evidence is in the letter knowledge pilot task sheet (in Spanish).
What our data show. Both tasks have very high internal consistency (α = .90 and .97). Letter naming is stable between terms (ρ = .73) and predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency years later with a median AUC of .71. As a skill with a ceiling, it discriminates mainly at ages 4 and 5.

title: Initial letter identification
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Initial letter identification” (codes 1884 and 4047; LEEDUCA battery) assesses alphabetic knowledge (phoneme–grapheme mapping). Each item is presented with a picture on the screen; the examiner gives the instruction orally and records the child’s response. It comprises 24 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2013, 2014 and 2015 cohorts it was administered in 6 sessions, from 5 to 7 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .90 (N = 3,273, 24 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .57. Stability across time points was ρ = .57. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .58–.69.

title: Reading for comprehension (second reading)
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading a continuous text measures reading fluency: reading accurately, at a good pace and with the intonation that the meaning requires. It integrates word recognition with sentence comprehension processes, which is why it is the bridge between decoding and comprehension in the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990). The platform measures two readings of the same story: the first, for speed, and a second aimed at comprehension.
What the evidence says:

Speed and comprehension go together in Spanish. In a transparent orthography, decoding is mastered early and its weight in comprehension decreases across school years, while that of oral language increases (Sánchez-Vincitore et al. 2022; Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018). Text reading speed is the decoding measure that remains related to comprehension the longest.
It is the most stable measure of reading skill in consistent orthographies. In German, slowness in Grade 1 anticipated slowness years later (Landerl and Wimmer 2008).
There are references in Spanish. The meta-analysis by Ripoll Salceda, Tapia Montesinos, and Aguado Alonso (2020) summarizes speeds by grade in Spanish speakers. Grade explains around 70% of the differences between studies, and speed changes with the term in the first school years.

What our data show. Stability between terms is ρ = .63 to .65. The 2021 α for text speed is low (.40), but α is not a good indicator for a timed task. It predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency with a median AUC of .74 to .75, and up to .84–.87 at the best time points. The comparison with the literature and the norms in words per minute are in the reading speed task sheet.

title: Reading for comprehension (second reading)
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .23–.80. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Reading comprehension (6.2, r = .08); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .30); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .27); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .15); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .29); Reading comprehension (8.1, r = .06); Phonological awareness (8.2, r = .38); Reading comprehension (9.2, r = -.10); Reading comprehension (10.2, r = -.06); Reading comprehension (11.2, r = -.11).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .67–.93 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .54–.65.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .54–.87 (7 time points; 122–591 children).

title: Reading for comprehension (second reading)
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Reading for comprehension (second reading)” (codes 10738, 10741, 2044, 2045, 3981 and 4098; EDICOLE battery) assesses reading rate when reading for comprehension. The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 11 items. The time limit is 60 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015 cohorts it was administered in 19 sessions, from 6 to 11 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .72 (median of 9 session pairs; range -0.47–.81). Stability across time points was ρ = .13–.77. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .54–.65.

title: Letter knowledge
text:
Theoretical framework
Letter knowledge is the ability to recognize each grapheme and associate it with its name or sound. It is the gateway to the alphabetic principle. The platform measures it in two ways: naming letters, and choosing the letter with which the name of a picture begins, which also requires isolating the first sound.
What the evidence says. Together with phonological awareness and rapid naming, it is one of the three major predictors of reading. Its weight is similar in English, Spanish and Czech (Caravolas et al. 2013). In Spanish, letter knowledge is the best predictor of simple syllable reading; phonological awareness weighs more for complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020). The full review of the evidence is in the letter knowledge pilot task sheet (in Spanish).
What our data show. Both tasks have very high internal consistency (α = .90 and .97). Letter naming is stable between terms (ρ = .73) and predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency years later with a median AUC of .71. As a skill with a ceiling, it discriminates mainly at ages 4 and 5.

title: Letter knowledge
text:
Validity
Concurrent. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Phonological awareness (4.2, r = .27); Phonological awareness (4.3, r = .32); Word and text reading (5.1, r = .70); Word and text reading (5.2, r = .67); Word and text reading (5.3, r = .70); Word and text reading (6.1, r = .72).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .69–.83. Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .57–.65.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .62–.76 (6 time points; 118–726 children).

Forms: can they be pooled?
Forms given at the same time point are compared. They are considered equivalent if the mean difference is smaller than 0.20 SD and the SD ratio is between 0.80 and 1.25. If the same children took them, linear equating is also computed, which puts the second form on the scale of the first, together with the correlation between forms (parallel-forms reliability). title: Letter knowledge
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Letter knowledge” (codes 1887, 535, 5431 and 67; LEEDUCA battery) assesses alphabetic knowledge. The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 52 items. The time limit is 60 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013 and 2014 cohorts it was administered in 17 sessions, from 4 to 6 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .97 (N = 2,127, 52 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .76 (median of 12 session pairs; range -0.06–.92). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .40–.93. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .57–.65.

The task has 3 forms; in 5 of 7 comparisons they have different scales. Norms are given by form (see “Forms”).

title: Word reading: one syllable
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Word reading: one syllable
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .62–.93. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Letter knowledge (5.1, r = .62); Phonological awareness (5.2, r = .52); Phonological awareness (5.3, r = .66); Phonological awareness (6.1, r = .64); Phonological awareness (6.2, r = .64); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .43).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .72–.94 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .58–.69.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .45–.78 (6 time points; 182–749 children).

title: Word reading: one syllable
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Word reading: one syllable” (code 69; LEEDUCA battery) assesses word reading (lexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 15 sessions, from 5 to 6 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .96 (N = 2,810, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .84 (median of 11 session pairs; range -0.39–.89). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .51–.89. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .58–.69.

title: Word reading: two syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Word reading: two syllables
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .62–.93. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Phonological awareness (5.2, r = .50); Phonological awareness (5.3, r = .60); Phonological awareness (6.1, r = .62); Phonological awareness (6.2, r = .60); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .35); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .44); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .18); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .23); Reading comprehension (8.1, r = .22); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .31).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .82–.94 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .55–.70.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .60–.79 (10 time points; 133–788 children).

title: Word reading: two syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Word reading: two syllables” (codes 1931, 71 and 73; LEEDUCA and DIS-ESP battery) assesses word reading (lexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 22 sessions, from 5 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .97 (N = 2,449, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .79 (median of 18 session pairs; range -0.33–.91). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .46–.90. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .55–.70.

title: Word reading: three syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Word reading: three syllables
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .57–.91. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Reading comprehension (6.2, r = .31); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .33); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .43); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .19); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .27); Phonological awareness (8.1, r = .41); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.2, r = .32); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .28).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .90–.95 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .50–.62.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .71–.81 (8 time points; 132–592 children).

title: Word reading: three syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Word reading: three syllables” (codes 1932 and 75; DIS-ESP battery) assesses word reading (lexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 15 sessions, from 6 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .93 (N = 639, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .80 (median of 12 session pairs; range .22–.85). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .42–.90. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .50–.62.

title: Word reading: four syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Word reading: four syllables
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .71–.86. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .17); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .26); Phonological awareness (8.1, r = .39); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.2, r = .48); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .31).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .87–.95 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .49–.59.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .74–.80 (5 time points; 241–592 children).

title: Word reading: four syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Word reading: four syllables” (code 1933; DIS-ESP battery) assesses word reading (lexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 9 sessions, from 7 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .86 (N = 3,251, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .80 (median of 6 session pairs; range .52–.83). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .64–.89. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .49–.59.

title: Pseudoword reading: two syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Pseudoword reading: two syllables
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .60–.93. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Letter knowledge (5.2, r = .64); Phonological awareness (5.3, r = .69); Phonological awareness (6.1, r = .60); Phonological awareness (6.2, r = .59); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .34); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .43); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .16); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .23); Reading comprehension (8.1, r = .22); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .33).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .81–.92 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .55–.65.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .69–.81 (8 time points; 133–783 children).

Forms: can they be pooled?
Forms given at the same time point are compared. They are considered equivalent if the mean difference is smaller than 0.20 SD and the SD ratio is between 0.80 and 1.25. If the same children took them, linear equating is also computed, which puts the second form on the scale of the first, together with the correlation between forms (parallel-forms reliability). title: Pseudoword reading: two syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Pseudoword reading: two syllables” (codes 1934, 72 and 74; LEEDUCA and DIS-ESP battery) assesses decoding (sublexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 19 sessions, from 5 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .96 (N = 1,156, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .74 (median of 15 session pairs; range .04–.88). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .43–.84. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .55–.65.

title: Pseudoword reading: three syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Pseudoword reading: three syllables
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .59–.85. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Reading comprehension (6.2, r = .29); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .32); Phonological awareness (7.1, r = .38); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .17); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .19); Phonological awareness (8.1, r = .47); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.2, r = .49); Rapid naming (RAN) (8.3, r = .28).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .86–.92 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .45–.61.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .69–.79 (8 time points; 241–592 children).

Forms: can they be pooled?
Forms given at the same time point are compared. They are considered equivalent if the mean difference is smaller than 0.20 SD and the SD ratio is between 0.80 and 1.25. If the same children took them, linear equating is also computed, which puts the second form on the scale of the first, together with the correlation between forms (parallel-forms reliability). title: Pseudoword reading: three syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Pseudoword reading: three syllables” (codes 1935 and 76; DIS-ESP battery) assesses decoding (sublexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 16 sessions, from 6 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .92 (N = 637, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .71 (median of 13 session pairs; range .44–.76). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .43–.80. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .45–.61.

title: Pseudoword reading: four syllables
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Pseudoword reading: four syllables
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Pseudoword reading: four syllables” (code 1936; DIS-ESP battery) assesses decoding (sublexical route). The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 8 sessions, from 7 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .73 (N = 3,187, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .69 (median of 5 session pairs; range .58–.71). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .42–.73. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .40–.56.

title: Complex syllable reading
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Complex syllable reading
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .69–.95. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Reading comprehension (6.2, r = .41); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .37); Reading comprehension (7.1, r = .28); Reading comprehension (7.2, r = .21); Reading comprehension (7.3, r = .21).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .85–.93 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .57–.63.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .71–.77 (5 time points; 264–562 children).

title: Complex syllable reading
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Complex syllable reading” (codes 2264 and 90; LEEDUCA battery) assesses decoding of complex syllables. The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 30 items. The time limit is 60 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 11 sessions, from 6 to 7 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .97 (N = 334, 30 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .72 (median of 7 session pairs; range .63–.85). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .55–.82. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .57–.63.

title: Simple syllable reading
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading syllables, words and pseudowords aloud measures written word recognition: converting letters into sounds and accessing the word. It is the decoding component of the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990) and the core of dyslexia according to the IDA definition (What we measure in light of the new definition of dyslexia).
What distinguishes each list. Dual-route models separate two procedures. The sublexical route converts graphemes into phonemes and is the only one that works for pseudowords. The lexical route recognizes the whole word, and it shows in words being read faster than pseudowords (lexicality effect) and frequent words faster than rare ones. In Spanish, children use both from Grade 2 (Avdyli, Castejón, and Cuetos 2014; Davies et al. 2013). That is why the platform has both lists: pseudowords measure pure decoding, and the difference with words estimates how much orthographic lexicon the child has built. Length (from one to four syllables) makes serial reading visible: the more the child depends on letter-by-letter conversion, the more each added syllable costs.
In a transparent orthography, what discriminates is speed. In Spanish, almost all children read accurately by the middle of Grade 1. Children with dyslexia are accurate but read more slowly, and their reading resembles that of younger children of the same reading level: it is delayed rather than deviant development (Davies, Cuetos, and Glez-Seijas 2007). A meta-analysis of 79 European studies concludes that reading speed distinguishes readers with dyslexia in all orthographies and ages, whereas accuracy depends on age and transparency (Carioti et al. 2021). In German, 70% of slow readers in Grade 1 were still slow in Year 8 (Landerl and Wimmer 2008). That is why the score in these task sheets is correct responses per minute, not correct responses.
What our data show. These are the most reliable and valid tasks on the platform:

Reliability. Stability between terms of ρ = .65 to .81, and 2021 α between .73 and .97.
External validity. They predict low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency years later with a median AUC of .72 to .77 (chapter, in Spanish). The longer lists (three- and four-syllable words) predict best.
Delay or deviance. Comparing pseudowords with words among children of the same reading level separates delay from deviance (Norms by reading level, in Spanish).

title: Simple syllable reading
text:
Validity
Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Word and text reading), r = .71–.87. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Letter knowledge (5.1, r = .73); Phonological awareness (5.2, r = .57); Letter knowledge (5.3, r = .48); Phonological awareness (6.1, r = .65); Reading comprehension (6.2, r = .48); Reading comprehension (6.3, r = .35).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .79–.92 (circular: agreement only). Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .50–.69.



Validity: AUC with 95% confidence interval (labels in Spanish).


Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .71–.77 (6 time points; 182–753 children).

Forms given at the same time point are compared. They are considered equivalent if the mean difference is smaller than 0.20 SD and the SD ratio is between 0.80 and 1.25. title: Simple syllable reading
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Simple syllable reading” (codes 2263 and 88; LEEDUCA battery) assesses decoding of simple syllables. The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 30 items. The time limit is 60 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 15 sessions, from 5 to 6 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .85 (N = 351, 30 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .77 (median of 11 session pairs; range .29–.92). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = .24–.92. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .50–.69.

title: Simple syllable reading
text:
Pending issues

Extreme value at 6.1 (form 2263): the maximum or minimum is more than 2 SD away from P99 or P1. Check in the raw data (possible timing or recording error).
Floor effect in the norms at 5.1 (form 2263) and 5.2 (form 2263): at least 10% of children have the worst possible score, so P10 does not exist. At those time points the “severe” and “very severe” levels must not be assigned with this task (study M3).
The task has 2 forms; in 1 of 2 comparisons they have different scales. Norms are given by form (see “Forms”).
The persistent difficulty label uses this task: validity against it is circular.
Write the interpretation; review with the team.

title: Text reading rate
text:
Theoretical framework
Reading a continuous text measures reading fluency: reading accurately, at a good pace and with the intonation that the meaning requires. It integrates word recognition with sentence comprehension processes, which is why it is the bridge between decoding and comprehension in the simple view of reading (Hoover and Gough 1990). The platform measures two readings of the same story: the first, for speed, and a second aimed at comprehension.
What the evidence says:

Speed and comprehension go together in Spanish. In a transparent orthography, decoding is mastered early and its weight in comprehension decreases across school years, while that of oral language increases (Sánchez-Vincitore et al. 2022; Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018). Text reading speed is the decoding measure that remains related to comprehension the longest.
It is the most stable measure of reading skill in consistent orthographies. In German, slowness in Grade 1 anticipated slowness years later (Landerl and Wimmer 2008).
There are references in Spanish. The meta-analysis by Ripoll Salceda, Tapia Montesinos, and Aguado Alonso (2020) summarizes speeds by grade in Spanish speakers. Grade explains around 70% of the differences between studies, and speed changes with the term in the first school years.

What our data show. Stability between terms is ρ = .63 to .65. The 2021 α for text speed is low (.40), but α is not a good indicator for a timed task. It predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency with a median AUC of .74 to .75, and up to .84–.87 at the best time points. The comparison with the literature and the norms in words per minute are in the reading speed task sheet.

title: Text reading rate
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Text reading rate” (codes 100, 10737, 10740, 1090, 2034, 2035, 3979 and 4099; EDICOLE and LEEDUCA battery) assesses reading fluency. The child reads aloud the stimuli shown on the screen and the examiner records each correct response or error. It comprises 60 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015 cohorts it was administered in 28 sessions, from 5 to 11 years of age. The main outcome is the efficiency (correct responses per unit of time). In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .40 (N = 859, 60 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .75 (median of 18 session pairs; range -0.54–.86). Because the task is timed, α tends to overestimate reliability; stability across administrations is the preferred estimate. Stability across time points was ρ = -.02–.86. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .48–.65.

title: Reading vocabulary
text:
Theoretical framework
Vocabulary is knowledge of word meanings. The platform measures it in two ways: orally, when the child explains the meaning of a word they hear, and through reading, when they choose, among three written words, the one with a similar meaning. In the simple view of reading, vocabulary is part of language comprehension, the component that does not depend on reading (Hoover and Gough 1990).
What the evidence says:

Preschool oral language predicts reading comprehension years later. Comprehension at age 8½ is explained by word reading at 5 and by language at 3½, in children at family risk of dyslexia and in the rest (Hulme et al. 2015). Language in the broad sense (vocabulary, grammar, inference) predicts it better than vocabulary alone (Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018).
Written vocabulary is not only language. Vocabulary tasks also capture variance from decoding, because the meaning, written form and phonology of each word are connected (Protopapas et al. 2013).
The relation is reciprocal. Reading more expands vocabulary, and a larger vocabulary makes it easier to read new words (Killingly et al. 2024). In the first school years the code (letters and phonological awareness) weighs more; later, word reading and comprehension separate (Storch and Whitehurst 2002).

What our data show. Vocabulary through reading predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency almost as well as the reading tasks (median AUC .75), but it is not very stable between terms (ρ = .43). Oral vocabulary at ages 4 and 5 has good internal consistency (α = .82) and predicts less (median AUC .63, maximum .71). This is to be expected: its main role is in comprehension, not fluency. It is also one of the best predictors of arithmetic at ages 10–11 (Numerical cognition, in Spanish).

title: Reading vocabulary
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Reading vocabulary” (code 1950; DIS-ESP battery) assesses reading vocabulary. The child reads silently and selects, among several on-screen options, the one that completes each item. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 6 sessions, from 7 to 10 years of age. The main outcome is the total score. Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 12 months) was ρ = .67. Stability across time points was ρ = .22–.63. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .51–.66.

title: Orthographic decision
text:
Theoretical framework
Choosing, between two forms that sound the same, the correctly spelled word (for example, vaca vs. baca) measures orthographic knowledge: the representations of specific words in the mental lexicon. This is what allows a word to be recognized at a glance, without converting it letter by letter.
How it is formed. According to the self-teaching hypothesis, each time the child successfully decodes a new word, something of its written form is stored. Phonological decoding works as an “internal teacher” (Jorm and Share 1983). Computational models show that this mechanism is enough to learn thousands of words and that initial phonological deficits are enough to produce dyslexia (Ziegler, Perry, and Zorzi 2014). A systematic review of 62 experiments confirms the role of phonological recoding in all writing systems (Li and Wang 2023). It also works in Spanish, except with infrequent spellings of a sound, which need more exposure (Ferroni and Diuk 2014).
What the task measures. Orthographic choice captures both knowledge of specific words and more general orthographic knowledge. Choosing correctly does not depend only on being able to read the word (Compton et al. 2020). In Spanish, the orthographic lexicon contributes to reading competence beyond decoding, and it is refined with years of practice (Cuadro and Costa 2014).
What our data show. 2021 α = .80 and stability between terms ρ = .52, lower than for reading aloud. Even so, it is one of the tasks that best predict low reading fluency years later (median AUC .76, maximum .80). This is to be expected if it measures how many words the child has consolidated, which is precisely what fails in dyslexia in a transparent orthography.

title: Orthographic decision
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Orthographic decision” (codes 1937 and 2039; DIS-ESP battery) assesses orthographic knowledge. The examiner presents each item orally, supported by a picture on the screen, and records the child’s oral response. It comprises 26 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010 and 2011 cohorts it was administered in 5 sessions, from 6 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .80 (N = 3,922, 26 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 8 months) was ρ = .63 (median of 3 session pairs; range .47–.66). Stability across time points was ρ = .43–.60. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .55–.61.

title: Phonological awareness: what makes a task difficult and how to read a failure
text:
Why start with speech
All of the platform’s phonological awareness tasks ask the child to reflect on the sounds of words they hear, and almost all ask them to respond by speaking. That is why, before interpreting a score, it helps to keep in mind how the phonological system of a child aged 4 to 7 is organized. The manual by Sánchez Gómez et al. (2026) summarizes it in three ideas that apply equally to phonological awareness.
1. The child learns contrasts, not sounds. A phoneme has no value in itself, but through the oppositions it establishes with others: pala/bala (voicing), tapa/capa (place of articulation), bala/mala (manner: oral versus nasal). Development consists of incorporating oppositions into the system. When a child says tasa for casa, the problem is not the sound /k/ but that the /k/–/t/ opposition is not yet operational in their system (Bosch 2004; Sánchez Gómez, Rodríguez, and López-Pérez 2026).
2. Speech goes through several levels. There is speech perception, phonological representation, planning and programming, and motor execution. The same surface error can arise at any of them, and the levels interact.
3. From symptom to mechanism. The manual distinguishes three levels of analysis, in line with models that separate symptoms, processes and causes (Sánchez Gómez, Rodríguez, and López-Pérez 2026):
Classifying is not attaching a label, but inferring the mechanism from the child’s productions.
Applied to the platform, a score on a phonological awareness task is a surface-level datum. What the manual wants to estimate lies at the proximal level: whether the child accesses the units of speech (syllables, phonemes) and can operate on them. Three factors come in between, which this chapter tries to separate:

text:
Five dimensions of difficulty
Research on phonological awareness, in English and in Spanish, agrees that the difficulty of a task depends mainly on five features (Carrillo 1994; Jiménez and Ortiz 2000; Anthony et al. 2003, 2011; Anthony and Lonigan 2004; Defior 2004). The platform makes it possible to see four of them with its own data.

① The unit: syllable before phoneme. The syllable is a unit the child perceives naturally in speech. The phoneme, on the other hand, is an abstraction largely built while learning to read, all the more so in a transparent orthography like Spanish (Carrillo 1994; Ziegler and Goswami 2005).
② The operation: recognizing before manipulating. From least to most demanding, the operations are:

detecting or matching (do they start the same?);
isolating (what sound does it start with?);
counting, segmenting and blending;
deleting (what is left if I remove…?).

Deletion requires holding the word in memory, removing a part and putting the rest back together (Anthony et al. 2003).
③ Position. In the English-language literature, the beginning of a word is usually easier to isolate than the end. On the platform, the effect of position depends on the operation:

For matching and isolating, the beginning is easier.
For deleting, removing the end is easier, because what remains keeps the beginning of the word and is often another word (patada → pata).

④ Structure and type of sound. Difficulty is influenced by:

complex syllables (CCV, CVC) versus simple ones (CV);
consonant clusters;
late-acquired phonemes (/r/, /ɾ/, /θ/, clusters with a liquid);
stop consonants, which cannot be prolonged, versus continuants (/s/, /f/, /m/), which are easier to isolate.

With the item-level data from the new platform (_res) this effect can be estimated item by item (see what is missing).
⑤ Response mode and lexical support.

Response mode. Pointing to a picture does not require speaking. Saying the initial phoneme, the remaining word or the resulting syllable does, and there phonological awareness and the child’s speech become mixed (see below).
Lexical support. Operating on known words is easier than on pseudowords (the “all positions” tasks at ages 7–8 use pseudowords).
Memory. Long words add memory load.
