What can be seen, with the caveat that each task has its own items and not always the same cohorts:

Unit. At ages 4–5, deleting an initial syllable is already within reach for half of the items (50% at 5.1), whereas deleting the initial phoneme stays at 37% at 5.2. At ages 7–8, once reading has been acquired, the gap between syllable and phoneme almost disappears in the pseudoword tasks (75% vs. 73% at 8.2). This is what the idea that phonemic awareness is largely built while learning to read in a transparent orthography predicts.
Operation. In the same term (5.2), isolating the initial phoneme (62%) is much easier than deleting it (37%).
Position. Matching by the initial syllable is easier than by the final one, once chance is discounted (64% vs. 16% at 4.2), and isolating the initial phoneme is easier than the final one (82% vs. 71% at 6.1). With deletion the opposite happens: removing the final syllable or phoneme is easier than removing the initial one.
Floors. The manipulation tasks have many children with zero correct just when they are introduced. Deleting the initial phoneme at age 5 has 28% of children at zero. Deleting the initial syllable at 4.2 has 25%. This fits the idea from the teaching manual that a unit or contrast is either operational or not: many children do not yet “see” the phoneme as a unit, rather than simply having low ability. That is why, at these ages, a zero is better read as “not yet accessible” than as one more percentile, and we propose that the norms and the risk classification treat it that way.

title: Phonological awareness: what makes a task difficult and how to read a failure
text:
What is missing

Within-child contrasts. Compare tasks of different unit, operation and position in the same children and in the same term, with an item model (Rasch or explanatory IRT) that estimates the effect of each dimension. It would replace the descriptive comparisons in this chapter. It can be done with the long table and, for the new platform, with the item-level responses (_res).
Item features. Code each item by syllable structure, type of phoneme (continuant or stop; early or late acquisition), length, frequency and dialect sensitivity (final /s/, /θ/, final liquids), and estimate how much of the difficulty they explain.
Receptive versus productive profile. Build an indicator comparing the tasks in which the child points (matching) with those that require saying sounds, and study whether it separates children with SSD from children at reading risk.
Speech on the platform. A brief speech record (or a teacher questionnaire) at ages 4 and 5 would make it possible to separate, in analysis, the speech component from the phonological awareness component, following the levels model of the teaching manual.

title: Phonological awareness: syllable counting
text:
Description
In one sentence. It is the phonological awareness task with the most children and cohorts on the platform: about 5,800 children from six cohorts. It measures what it intends to: it is related mainly to other phonological awareness tasks, it has no floor and hardly any ceiling at age 4. But on its own it is a weak measure: it is not very stable from one school year to the next (r ≈ .35) and it predicts persistent reading difficulty poorly (AUC ≈ .65). It should not be used alone to classify a child. Its natural place is within a phonological awareness composite.
The examiner names the picture that appears on the screen and the child says how many syllables (“little pieces”) the word has. The examiner marks the number with the mouse. There are 20 items.
It was given on the old platform (until 2017/18) and on the new one (from 2018/19), with the same results on both (table of descriptive statistics by cohort).

title: Phonological awareness: syllable counting
text:
Theoretical framework and evidence
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech: words, syllables, rhymes and phonemes. With letter knowledge and rapid naming it forms the classic triad of reading predictors. Counting syllables is one of the easiest tasks on the continuum: it requires segmenting a spoken word into syllables, without removing or changing anything.
What the evidence says:

The phoneme level is the most predictive. In a meta-analysis of 235 studies, phonemic awareness was the strongest correlate of word reading, above rhyme and verbal memory (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012). In longitudinal studies in German, another language with a transparent orthography, the mean relation with later reading was r = .31, and it was also larger at the phoneme level than at the rhyme level (Pfost, 2015).
One skill, many levels of difficulty. In more than 1,200 Spanish-speaking children aged 3 to 6, phonological awareness tasks (word, syllable and phoneme; blending and elision) measure a single general skill, with items of very different difficulty. The stability of the skill over that period was r = .64 (Anthony et al., 2011).
The role of the syllable in Spanish. Sensitivity to the syllable appears early and may be especially important in Spanish (Denton et al., 2000). In 5-year-olds, syllable blending was the task that best predicted reading one year later (Fumagalli et al., 2014). Fine-grained segmental awareness, on the other hand, develops mainly when learning the alphabetic code (Carrillo, 1994).
In Spanish, letters weigh heavily. In children aged 5 to 7, letter knowledge was the best predictor of reading simple syllables, and phonological awareness only predicted reading complex syllables (Martínez & Goikoetxea, 2020). There are even doubts about how much teaching phonemic awareness contributes for children learning to read in Spanish (Goldenberg et al., 2014).
It can be trained, and training shows in reading. In Spanish speakers, phonological awareness interventions improve reading accuracy (combined d ≈ 0.36; Ripoll & Zevallos, 2023). The causal effect is better established for phonemic awareness combined with letter–sound knowledge (Hulme et al., 2012).

What our data say:

Syllable counting behaves like an easy task on the continuum: it is more closely related to other phonological awareness tasks than to any other domain, but it predicts reading difficulty less than letters and adds almost nothing over letters and rapid naming. This fits the literature: at ages 4–5, the syllable level is the least informative, and in Spanish letters take a good part of the prediction.
Stability from age 4 to 5 (r ≈ .35) is far below that of the general skill in Anthony et al. (2011). This is to be expected with a single 20-item task: the error of a single task is large, and a composite reduces it.

References located with SciSpace (volumes and pages still to be checked): Anthony et al. (2011), Journal of Educational Psychology; Carrillo (1994), Reading and Writing; Denton et al. (2000), Reading Psychology; Fumagalli et al. (2014), Revista Argentina de Ciencias del Comportamiento; Goldenberg et al. (2014), American Educational Research Journal; Hulme et al. (2012), Psychological Science; Martínez & Goikoetxea (2020), Psicología Educativa, 26(1); Melby-Lervåg et al. (2012), Psychological Bulletin; Pfost (2015), Zeitschrift für Entwicklungspsychologie und Pädagogische Psychologie; Ripoll & Zevallos (2023), Revista de Investigación en Logopedia.

Syllable counting norms: P10–P90, P25–P75, median and P16 (labels in Spanish).



Distribution. At age 4, median of 10 correct, almost symmetrical, with no floor (≈ 3% with 0) and no ceiling (≈ 3% with 20). At age 5, median of 14, with 12% at ceiling: the task begins to fall short for the best children.
Reliability. The correlation between 4.1 and 5.1 in the same children is .33–.40 in three cohorts. It is low for a 20-item task: part of it is due to real change during a year of rapid development, but it also indicates considerable error. Internal consistency (α, ω) is pending: the long table does not have the item-level responses for this task.
Concurrent validity. It is more closely related to other phonological awareness tasks at the same time point (r = .40–.46) than to vocabulary (.11–.25), letters (.29) or rapid naming (.08–.16). This is the expected pattern.
Predictive validity. Against persistent reading difficulty from age 6 to 11, the AUC is .66 at age 4 and .64 at age 5. Below P25 it detects 40% of future cases with 20% false positives.
Incremental validity. Over letters and rapid naming, it adds very little: +0.005 in AUC at age 4 and +0.002 at age 5, with cross-validation.
Variables that affect it. Relative age weighs at age 4 (d = 0.44 between children born in the first and second half of the year) and less at age 5 (d = 0.24). School socioeconomic status weighs little (d = 0.26 at age 4; null at age 5). Schools explain 14–19% of the variance.







Continuous norms and floor effect (study M3, November 3, 2026)



Syllable counting is a count of 0 to 20 correct responses, so GAMLSS needs a discrete distribution (beta-binomial). With it, it is the best method out of sample (mean error of 1.4 percentile points), and all methods are within 2.3 points of the nominal P10. Floor: 4% with zero correct at 4.1.

title: Rapid automatized naming (RAN)
text:
1. Task description
Main finding. In the same children and in the same session, digit RAN predicts persistent reading difficulty better than color RAN: AUC 0.76 vs. 0.70 at age 4 (p = .046) and 0.74 vs. 0.67 at age 5 (p = .014, DeLong test for paired curves). At age 4, digit RAN adds information to phonological awareness and letters (OR = 2.0 per SD; +0.03 in AUC with cross-validation). At age 5 it no longer adds anything.
Consequence for article L2. The RAN composite used by the certainty labels and by L2 averages all RAN tasks at each time point, including versions with a different scoring format. It predicts considerably worse than digit RAN alone (AUC 0.65 and 0.62; p ≤ .001). This explains, at least in part, why RAN “added nothing” in L2. The age-4 model of L2 must be rerun with digit RAN.
Task sheet generated with scripts/R/ficha_RAN.R (output DIAGNOSTICO/R/ficha_RAN_R_v1.xlsx), with the same structure as the letters and reading speed pilot sheets. Aggregated data; non-Preleo reference except where indicated.
The child names aloud, as fast as possible, very familiar stimuli that appear on the screen one at a time (discrete format). The examiner presses the left mouse button if the response is correct and the right one if it is wrong; pressing brings up the next stimulus. The platform records correct responses, errors and total time.
Main measure: efficiency, in items named correctly per minute (correct × 60 / time). It is the same unit as in the letters task sheet and the words per minute of the reading speed task sheet, and it captures speed and accuracy at once. Total time is also given for comparison with the literature.
Discrete versus card format. Classic RAN is administered on a card: all stimuli at once, named serially by the child. The platform version presents one stimulus at a time, and the time includes the examiner’s key press. This is an important difference when interpreting results (section 1 bis).

title: Rapid automatized naming (RAN)
text:
1 bis. Theoretical framework
Rapid automatized naming (RAN) measures how fast a child retrieves and articulates the names of very familiar stimuli. With phonological awareness and letter knowledge it forms the classic triad of reading predictors. The double-deficit hypothesis (Wolf & Bowers, 1999) proposed that slow RAN is a core of dyslexia distinct from the phonological deficit, and that children with both deficits have the most severe difficulties. Maryanne Wolf also created RAS, a version that alternates letters, digits and colors and adds flexibility in name retrieval (Wolf, Reader, Come Home).
What the evidence says:

It predicts beyond phonological awareness. In a meta-analysis of RAN before primary school (60 samples, 10,513 children), RAN is related to later reading with r = −.38 and contributes uniquely after controlling for phonological awareness (semipartial r = −.25) (McWeeny et al., 2022).
Alphanumeric better than non-alphanumeric. RAN of digits and letters predicts more than RAN of colors or objects (McWeeny et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021). In Spanish schoolchildren in Grades 2 to 6, RAN tasks form two factors, alphanumeric and non-alphanumeric (Rodríguez et al., 2015).
Discrete versus card format. In Grade 1, card RAN is more closely related to reading than discrete RAN (de Jong, 2011). The card requires chaining stimuli, which resembles reading a line of text. The discrete format mainly measures retrieval of each stimulus’s name.

What our data say:

With the discrete format, digit RAN predicts reading difficulty with an AUC of 0.74–0.76, close to what letters and phonological awareness achieve at these ages.
It is confirmed that alphanumeric RAN predicts better than non-alphanumeric RAN, and moreover in the same children, which is uncommon in the literature.
At age 4, digits and colors share only 34% of their variance (r = .58–.60). There is a common naming-speed component and another specific to each type of stimulus.
At age 4, naming the digits 1–4 also requires knowing them: four in ten children (41%) make some error (a mean of 2.3 errors in 20 items; for colors, 29% and 1.2). Part of its predictive power may come from that symbol knowledge, as with letters.

References: Chen et al. (2021), Reading and Writing, doi:10.1007/s11145-021-10160-7; de Jong (2011), Scientific Studies of Reading, doi:10.1080/10888438.2010.485624; McWeeny et al. (2022), Reading Research Quarterly, doi:10.1002/rrq.467; Rodríguez et al. (2015), Scientific Studies of Reading, doi:10.1080/10888438.2015.1025271; Wolf & Bowers (1999), Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(3). Located with SciSpace; volumes and pages still to be checked.

text:
6. Studies it opens up
The platform contains “implicit experiments”: comparisons that the design of the sessions makes possible without having been planned. Each study shows its type and what is already available.










#
Study
Type
Question
What is already available




E1
L2 with cleaned RAN
Hypothesis test
Does the age-4 model of L2 improve if the RAN composite is replaced by cleaned digit RAN?
AUC 0.76 vs. 0.65 for the composite (§ 4.3). The full model still needs to be rerun.


E2
Speed versus symbol knowledge
Theoretical
At age 4, does digit RAN predict because of naming speed or because of knowing the digits? Correct responses and time per correct response are separated.
Correct responses and time per child (2011, 2014).


E3
Alphanumeric versus non-alphanumeric
Implicit experiment
Same session, same children, two types of stimulus. Does the advantage of digits hold in two-factor models (Rodríguez et al., 2015)?
2,200 children with both variants (§ 4.3).


E4
Discrete versus card
Methodological
Does the card format predict more, as de Jong (2011) found?
Card versions 2093/2094 exist, but their data are not valid. It can be proposed for the new platform.


E5
RAS (alternating letters, digits and colors)
Hypothesis test
Does alternation (flexibility, control) add anything to simple RAN, as Wolf proposes?
No data. Proposal for a new task.


E6
Item-level times
Methodological
α/ω of naming times; time curve across the task (fatigue, learning); items that fail most.
New platform, 2014 cohort (_di, _res).


E7
Relative age and RAN
Exploratory
Does the effect of relative age on RAN (d ≈ 0.4 at age 4) explain part of the overidentification of children born late in the year?
Effects by time point (§ 5.2); same logic as the letters task sheet.


E8
Double deficit in Spanish
Theoretical
Do children with slow RAN and low phonological awareness have the worst prognosis (Wolf & Bowers, 1999)?
RAN, phonological awareness and reading criterion in the same children (2010, 2011).


E9
The triad
Theoretical and applied
Letters, phonological awareness and RAN: how much each contributes by age. At age 4 RAN contributes; at age 5 it does not (§ 4.4).
Incremental validity in this task sheet; letters and speed task sheets.



Utility of each result.

Scientific: E2, E3, E8 and E9 test theoretical hypotheses with large samples in a transparent language.
Educational: digit RAN at age 4 is brief and does not require being able to read. It helps guide classroom support before reading problems appear.
Clinical: in a profile with phonological awareness and letters, slow RAN at age 4 almost doubles the risk. At age 5 it is descriptive information, not an added predictor.







Continuous norms and floor effect (study M3, November 3, 2026)



For object RAN with phoneme (1925), continuous methods are more stable than the table by time point (up to 30% less variation in P10 between two halves of the sample), but there are no data between 5.2 and 6.2 and the cNORM polynomial collapses in that gap. Until there are data for 5.3–6.1, the continuous norms should not be interpolated in that range. RAN has no floor effect (times do not pile up at the maximum).
Details in study M3.

title: Syllable counting
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Syllable counting
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Syllable counting” (code 523; LEEDUCA battery) assesses syllable awareness (segmentation). Each item is presented with a picture on the screen; the examiner gives the instruction orally and records the child’s response. It comprises 20 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 and 2015 cohorts it was administered in 9 sessions, from 4 to 5 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .86 (N = 2,202, 20 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 12 months) was ρ = .34 (median of 3 session pairs; range .32–.40). Stability across time points was ρ = .33–.40. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .57–.65.

title: Final phoneme isolation
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Final phoneme isolation
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Final phoneme isolation” (code 1897; LEEDUCA battery) assesses phonemic awareness (final phoneme isolation). The child selects a response among the options presented on the screen. It comprises 10 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 4 sessions, from 5 to 6 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .86 (N = 2,321, 10 items). Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .59–.63.

Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Initial phoneme isolation
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Initial phoneme isolation” (codes 1675 and 1896; LEEDUCA battery) assesses phonemic awareness (initial phoneme isolation). The child selects a response among the options presented on the screen. It comprises 11 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2013 and 2014 cohorts it was administered in 6 sessions, from 5 to 6 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .92 (N = 1,546, 11 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 8 months) was ρ = .43 (median of 2 session pairs; range .40–.47). Stability across time points was ρ = .27. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .56–.61.

title: Phoneme segmentation
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .70–.76. Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .56–.65.

Against an external criterion, years later. Against low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency in 2021/22 (chapter, in Spanish), AUC .60–.67 (3 time points; 265–508 children).

title: Phoneme segmentation
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Phoneme segmentation” (codes 1890 and 2017; LEEDUCA battery) assesses phonemic awareness (segmentation). Each item is presented with a picture on the screen; the examiner gives the instruction orally and records the child’s response. It comprises 10 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012, 2014 and 2015 cohorts it was administered in 8 sessions, from 5 to 7 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .84 (N = 1,640, 10 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 4 months) was ρ = .53 (median of 2 session pairs; range .51–.54). Stability across time points was ρ = .36–.46. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .56–.65.

title: Phoneme deletion (all positions)
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Phoneme deletion (all positions)” (codes 1940 and 2009; LEEDUCA and DIS-ESP battery) assesses phonemic awareness (deletion). The child selects a response among the options presented on the screen. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 240 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 5 sessions, from 6 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .87 (N = 922, 12 items). Stability across successive administrations (median interval of 8 months) was ρ = .50. title: Final phoneme deletion
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Initial phoneme deletion
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

Concurrent. With other tasks in its own domain (Phonological awareness), r = .55–.61. Outside its domain, the highest relation is with: Oral morphosyntax (5.2, r = .30); Word and text reading (5.3, r = .53).
Against reading difficulty and comprehension. Against persistent difficulty, AUC .67–.73. Against poor comprehension one or two school years later (non-circular criterion), AUC .58–.62.

title: Initial phoneme deletion
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Initial phoneme deletion” (code 1552; LEEDUCA battery) assesses phonemic awareness (initial phoneme deletion). Each item is presented with a picture on the screen; the examiner gives the instruction orally and records the child’s response. It comprises 10 items. The time limit is 120 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 3 sessions, from 5 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .94 (N = 1,232, 10 items). Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .58–.62.

title: Syllable deletion (all positions)
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Syllable deletion (all positions)
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Syllable deletion (all positions)” (code 1941; DIS-ESP battery) assesses syllable awareness (deletion). Stimuli are presented auditorily and the child responds by selecting on the screen. It comprises 14 items. The time limit is 240 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 4 sessions, from 7 to 8 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .82 (N = 1,554, 14 items). Stability across time points was ρ = .40. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .50–.60.

title: Initial syllable deletion
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Deletion of the syllable /xa/
text:
Theoretical framework
Phonological awareness is the ability to reflect on and manipulate the sounds of speech. The platform’s tasks cover a continuum of difficulty:

by unit: syllable or phoneme;
by operation: counting, identifying, segmenting or deleting;
by position: initial, final or any.

The “all positions” version mixes items and is the most demanding.
What the evidence says:

Phonemes and manipulation are what most distinguish dyslexia. In 2,252 children from six European languages, phoneme deletion and RAN were the strongest concurrent predictors of dyslexia (Landerl et al. 2013). In consistent orthographies, children with dyslexia perform below even younger readers of the same reading level on phoneme manipulation tasks, but not on syllable tasks (Parrila et al. 2020).
In Spanish, phonological awareness develops in stages, from the syllable to the phoneme. Phonemic awareness builds on learning to read and at the same time drives it: the relation is reciprocal (Denton et al. 2000). Phonological awareness predicts above all the reading of complex syllables (Martínez and Goikoetxea 2020).
Its predictive value is universal, but changes with age. Phonemic awareness, letters and RAN predict reading growth equally in Spanish, Czech and English (Caravolas et al. 2013). Its relation with fluency, however, is more complex and depends on task and age, whereas RAN predicts fluency in all languages (Landerl et al. 2019). This is what Catts, Haynes, and Joshi (2026) lead us to expect: precursors are useful for early prognosis and lose weight once there is reading to measure.

The pilot task sheets develop this framework in more detail: syllable counting and rapid naming (in Spanish).
What our data show. The pattern matches the literature:

What predicts best. Deletion tasks in all positions are those that best predict low Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (median AUC .72–.73, up to .81).
In between. The other deletion and identification tasks (.63–.68).
What predicts least. Phoneme segmentation and syllable counting (.60–.62).
Consistency and stability. Internal consistency is good (α = .82–.94), but stability between terms is low (ρ = .27–.41). Many tasks were given in only one or two sessions, and children change quickly at these ages. For an individual decision, the result should be confirmed at two time points.

title: Deletion of the syllable /xa/
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Deletion of the syllable /xa/” (code 1886; LEEDUCA battery) assesses syllable awareness (deletion in any position). Each item is presented with a picture on the screen; the examiner gives the instruction orally and records the child’s response. It comprises 12 items. The time limit is 240 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 3 sessions, from 6 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .93 (N = 2,354, 12 items). Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .58–.62.

title: Vocabulary: definitions
text:
Theoretical framework
Vocabulary is knowledge of word meanings. The platform measures it in two ways: orally, when the child explains the meaning of a word they hear, and through reading, when they choose, among three written words, the one with a similar meaning. In the simple view of reading, vocabulary is part of language comprehension, the component that does not depend on reading (Hoover and Gough 1990).
What the evidence says:

Preschool oral language predicts reading comprehension years later. Comprehension at age 8½ is explained by word reading at 5 and by language at 3½, in children at family risk of dyslexia and in the rest (Hulme et al. 2015). Language in the broad sense (vocabulary, grammar, inference) predicts it better than vocabulary alone (Lervåg, Hulme, and Melby-Lervåg 2018).
Written vocabulary is not only language. Vocabulary tasks also capture variance from decoding, because the meaning, written form and phonology of each word are connected (Protopapas et al. 2013).
The relation is reciprocal. Reading more expands vocabulary, and a larger vocabulary makes it easier to read new words (Killingly et al. 2024). In the first school years the code (letters and phonological awareness) weighs more; later, word reading and comprehension separate (Storch and Whitehurst 2002).

What our data show. Vocabulary through reading predicts low Woodcock-Muñoz reading fluency almost as well as the reading tasks (median AUC .75), but it is not very stable between terms (ρ = .43). Oral vocabulary at ages 4 and 5 has good internal consistency (α = .82) and predicts less (median AUC .63, maximum .71). This is to be expected: its main role is in comprehension, not fluency. It is also one of the best predictors of arithmetic at ages 10–11 (Numerical cognition, in Spanish).

text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Vocabulary: definitions” (code 1705; BUIZA battery) assesses expressive vocabulary. The child selects a response among the options presented on the screen. It comprises 20 items. The time limit is 150 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 3 sessions, from 4 to 5 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .81 (N = 580, 20 items). Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .57–.64.

title: Numerical cognition
text: Theoretical framework: learning mathematics and dyscalculia

title: Numerical cognition
text:
What dyscalculia is
Developmental dyscalculia is a neurodevelopmental disorder that specifically and persistently affects mathematics learning, especially understanding quantities, counting and calculation, despite adequate schooling and average intelligence. The DSM-5-TR includes it as specific learning disorder with impairment in mathematics (American Psychiatric Association 2022), and ICD-11 as developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics (Organización Mundial de la Salud 2019). It affects 3 to 7% of schoolchildren, a proportion similar to that of dyslexia, and its consequences are at least as serious, although it receives much less attention (Butterworth, Varma, and Laurillard 2011).
Like dyslexia, it is dimensional: it is the low end of a continuum of ability, and the same genes that influence normal differences in mathematics influence the disorder (Kovas et al. 2007). It also persists into adulthood if there is no intervention.


Number sense
The foundation is number sense: the ability, present even in infants, to perceive and compare quantities approximately. It shows in three phenomena:

Subitizing: up to three or four items are perceived at a glance, without counting.
Distance effect: it is easier to decide which of two numbers is larger the further apart they are (8 vs. 2 is easier than 8 vs. 7).
Mental number line: numbers are represented in space, from smaller to larger. At first that line is compressed (distances between large numbers seem smaller) and with instruction it becomes linear. Accuracy in placing numbers on a line predicts later mathematics achievement (Booth and Siegler 2006).

The triple-code model distinguishes three formats of number, with partly different brain circuits: magnitude, in the intraparietal sulcus of both hemispheres; the verbal code (number words and memorized arithmetic facts), in the left angular gyrus; and the Arabic code (digits) (Dehaene et al. 2003).


How it develops
The model of von Aster and Shalev (2007) describes four linked steps, each building on the previous one and with greater working memory demands:

Magnitude system: concrete quantities, subitizing and comparison (from infancy).
Verbal system: counting with number words, counting strategies and fact retrieval (preschool).
Arabic system: digits, written calculation (school).
Mental number line: ordinality, approximate calculation and arithmetic reasoning (school).

To count correctly, five principles must be mastered: one-to-one correspondence, stable order, cardinality (the last number said is the total), abstraction and order irrelevance (Gelman and Gallistel 1978). With practice, calculation moves from counting all (2 + 3: “one, two, three, four, five”) to counting on from the larger (“three, four, five”), to decomposing and, finally, to retrieving the result from memory.


What fails in dyscalculia
Children with dyscalculia use immature calculation strategies for longer and have difficulty retrieving arithmetic facts from memory (Geary 2004). The difficulties cluster along four axes:

Magnitude representation: comparing quantities and placing numbers on the line is slower and less precise. For many authors this is the core deficit, which spreads to the following steps (Aster and Shalev 2007; Butterworth, Varma, and Laurillard 2011).
Counting: the principles are mastered later and finger counting persists longer.
Memory for number facts: few results become automatic, partly because frequent errors give few opportunities to practice the correct one.
Working memory and attention: errors in holding numbers while operating, and more errors the more operations are carried out at once.

The proposed subtypes (procedural, semantic memory, visuospatial and number sense) have not been confirmed as clearly separate categories (Geary 2004). As with dyslexia, the most accepted explanation is multilevel: genetic factors, development of the intraparietal sulcus and its connections, a deficit in the representation of quantities and, finally, difficulties in calculation and problem solving (Butterworth, Varma, and Laurillard 2011).


Dyslexia and dyscalculia together
The two difficulties co-occur more than would be expected by chance. They share risk factors, such as rapid naming and verbal memory, which affect arithmetic facts memorized in verbal format, and each also has its own factors: phonological awareness in reading and magnitude representation in mathematics (Koponen et al. 2013). That is why the same screening can look for both. The platform data on this comorbidity are below.

For intervention, the evidence supports intensive, adaptive work on magnitude and its link with symbols, as in the program The Number Race (Wilson et al. 2006).

The response format changes. At ages 5–6 the child solves the operation and the examiner marks correct or incorrect (2005). Timed tasks are scored by efficiency, so the number of items in the activity is a ceiling, not the actual length of the test.
The “mental line” (1745) is a different task: estimating on a number line, not comparing magnitudes. It needs to be separated from non-symbolic magnitudes in the dictionary.

title: Numerical cognition
section: What is already known from these data

title: Numerical cognition
text:
Validity against arithmetic at ages 10–11
For reading, the manual has an external criterion, Woodcock-Muñoz fluency (chapter). For mathematics there is neither an external test nor school grades. The provisional criterion is arithmetic at ages 10–11: two-digit addition and subtraction, in the 2021/22 session, 2010 and 2011 cohorts (809 children). It is the same task used in the definition of dyscalculia risk by Loredo et al. “Low arithmetic” means being at −1 SD or below the mean of one’s cohort (14% of the sample). With the definition of Loredo et al. (low in arithmetic and in symbolic magnitudes), the risk of dyscalculia is 4.6%, very close to the published 4.2%.
Each earlier task from the same children is compared with two criteria: low arithmetic and low reading fluency. If the tasks have discriminant validity, the numerical ones should predict mathematics better and the reading ones, reading.

What the data say:

Reading has discriminant validity; mathematics does not yet. Reading tasks predict low reading fluency much better (median AUC 0.74) than low arithmetic (0.61). Numerical tasks predict low arithmetic barely as well as low reading (0.59 vs. 0.58), and no better than the reading tasks.
Some numerical tasks are specific. Counting backward in the second ten at age 5 predicts low arithmetic (AUC 0.67) and not low reading (0.51). Counting from 1 to 10 and non-symbolic magnitude comparison at age 4 show the same, weaker pattern. Single-digit addition at age 6 is the best numerical predictor (0.71), but it predicts reading equally well or better.
Comorbidity appears here too. Of the 799 children with both criteria, 19 have low arithmetic and low fluency at the same time, whereas 12 would be expected by chance. 17% of children with low arithmetic also have low reading fluency. With the stricter definition of Loredo et al., that proportion rises to half.

Why the criterion is weak. There are three reasons, and all three point to the criterion more than to the tasks:

it is a single, timed task, group-administered on tablets, with no known reliability in that administration;
arithmetic at age 11 is very far from the preschool tasks: what is required changes in between (mental calculation, written procedures), so it is a distant criterion;
timed addition and subtraction also require processing speed and number reading, which it shares with reading.

Testing a composite criterion (arithmetic + symbolic magnitudes) did not change the results.

text:
What is missing for them to enter the manual with full task sheets

Separate the versions of symbolic magnitudes and of the codes with two tasks (10759).
Compute α or ω with the item-level responses of the new platform (2018 onwards), especially for the 2021/22 tasks.
Improve the validity criterion. Arithmetic at ages 10–11 remains a provisional criterion. There are two ways to get a better one:

a closer criterion: arithmetic and magnitudes at ages 6–7;
an external mathematics test in a subsample, for example the BERDE battery once it is digitized.

Task sheets by family. The counting and number-reading tasks are accuracy tasks (family A). Magnitude comparison is decision with response time (family E). Timed addition and subtraction are efficiency tasks and need their own score (correct in 1 minute).

title: Counting backwards (1–10)
text:
Theoretical framework
Counting forwards and backwards, and reading Arabic numerals, measure symbolic number knowledge: the verbal sequence of numerals and its correspondence with digits. This is learned knowledge, distinct from the approximate number sense (comparing quantities), and it forms the basis of school arithmetic.
What the evidence says:

Counting in preschool predicts mathematics in the first school years. Mastery of counting principles at age 5 predicts the risk of mathematical difficulties in Grade 1 (Stock, Desoete, and Roeyers 2009). In Spanish children, the verbal number sequence (procedural counting) was the preschool task with the most weight in Grade 2 mathematics achievement (Mercader Ruiz, Presentación Herrero, and Siegenthaler Hierro 2017).
Knowing Arabic numerals is one of the two pillars of early arithmetic. In 569 children, only number knowledge and quantity discrimination uniquely predicted arithmetic progress in the first school year (Malone, Burgoyne, and Hulme 2020). Children with mathematical difficulties already show symbolic deficits in preschool, and those deficits persist (Desoete et al. 2012).
Counting backwards is more demanding than counting forwards. It requires retrieving the sequence in reverse order and holding it in working memory, which is why it discriminates better at age 5.

What our data show. The four tasks have high internal consistency (α = .84–.95), but they were given in one or two sessions and there is no stability between terms. They predict later reading fluency poorly (AUC .53–.59), which supports their discriminant validity. Against low arithmetic at ages 10–11, counting backwards in the second ten is the most specific: AUC .67 vs. .51 for reading (Numerical cognition, in Spanish).

title: Counting backwards (1–10)
text:
For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Counting backwards (1–10)” (code 2031; LEEDUCA battery) assesses verbal number sequence. The child names a series of familiar stimuli on the screen as quickly as possible, and the examiner records correct responses and errors. It comprises 6 items. The time limit is 30 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2011 and 2012 cohorts it was administered in 2 sessions, from 5 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .95 (N = 1,231, 6 items). Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .57–.59.

title: Counting forwards (11–20)
text:
Theoretical framework
Counting forwards and backwards, and reading Arabic numerals, measure symbolic number knowledge: the verbal sequence of numerals and its correspondence with digits. This is learned knowledge, distinct from the approximate number sense (comparing quantities), and it forms the basis of school arithmetic.
What the evidence says:

Counting in preschool predicts mathematics in the first school years. Mastery of counting principles at age 5 predicts the risk of mathematical difficulties in Grade 1 (Stock, Desoete, and Roeyers 2009). In Spanish children, the verbal number sequence (procedural counting) was the preschool task with the most weight in Grade 2 mathematics achievement (Mercader Ruiz, Presentación Herrero, and Siegenthaler Hierro 2017).
Knowing Arabic numerals is one of the two pillars of early arithmetic. In 569 children, only number knowledge and quantity discrimination uniquely predicted arithmetic progress in the first school year (Malone, Burgoyne, and Hulme 2020). Children with mathematical difficulties already show symbolic deficits in preschool, and those deficits persist (Desoete et al. 2012).
Counting backwards is more demanding than counting forwards. It requires retrieving the sequence in reverse order and holding it in working memory, which is why it discriminates better at age 5.

What our data show. The four tasks have high internal consistency (α = .84–.95), but they were given in one or two sessions and there is no stability between terms. They predict later reading fluency poorly (AUC .53–.59), which supports their discriminant validity. Against low arithmetic at ages 10–11, counting backwards in the second ten is the most specific: AUC .67 vs. .51 for reading (Numerical cognition, in Spanish).

For publications

For publications
The LEEDUCA platform task “Inhibition” (code 1863; UNED battery) assesses inhibitory control. The child names a series of familiar stimuli on the screen as quickly as possible, and the examiner records correct responses and errors. It comprises 121 items. The time limit is 300 seconds. It is administered individually on a computer at school. In the 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 cohorts it was administered in 6 sessions, from 4 to 7 years of age. The main outcome is the number of correct responses. In our data (2021 analyses), internal consistency was α = .98 (N = 2,501, 121 items). Stability across time points was ρ = .05. Against later poor reading comprehension, AUC = .46–.51.

title: Glossary (Spanish–English)
text:
School and sample
This glossary fixes how the manual’s Spanish terms are rendered in English. Every term in the table is always translated the same way. It also helps readers who move between the English edition, the Spanish version and the platform’s own reports, which are in Spanish. The list is kept in traduccion/glosario_es_en.csv in the repository.
School system. In Spain, Educación Infantil (preschool) covers ages 3 to 5 and primary school starts at age 6. Systematic reading instruction begins in Grade 1. The school year has three terms (autumn, winter, spring). A time point such as 5.2 means age 5, winter term.
